years before joining CMIS, the Mathematics and Information

industrial research organization in 1999.

messages.subject: [S] Finding common elements in two data frames
messages.subject_clean: [S] Finding common elements in two data frames
messages.body_plain:
I am using Splus 4.5 in an NT environment.

I have two data frames one with 329 records, and the other with 314
records. I need to subset the larger of the two data frames, retaining
only records that have a corresponding record in the smaller frame.  All
suggestions will be much appreciated.

For instance
attach(large.frame)
objects(2)
[1]  "diam", "zone", "species"

detach("large.frame")

attach(small frame)
objects(2)
[1] "diam", zone, "species"

What I need to do is make a data frame that has records for each "zone"
but only if the zone is included in the small frame.

Thanks

Steve Friedman

messages.subject: [S] Global minimization function in C?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I was wondering whether someone could point me to a global minimization
function (such as Simulated Annealing) coded in C or C++. My problem
lies in minimizing random functions that are discontinuous and have a
lot of local minima where "standard" minimization functions (such as
Golden Section Search) tend to get stuck.

For the moment, my functions are univariate (in case there should be
some easier functions available for this situation) but in the future I
might also have to consider multivariate functions. In all cases, the
arguments of the functions lie in compact sets.

Please (also) respond to me directly, since I am not subscribed to the
list. In case there is any interest, I am more than happy to post a
summary.

Thanks much,
Michael

messages.body_plain:
Dear S-Plus users

I am working with S-Plus 2000 for Win NT4 on a Pentium III 733 MHz
machine with 1 GB RAM.

Sorrowly, during a calculation S-Plus crashed with an error (I forgot to
write it down) and the problem now is that I can no longer open the
directory I was working in and thus lost all my data. (Whenever I try
to open the directory S-Plus crashes again)

Question 1: 
Is there a way to recover the directory, i.e. the database "_Data"?

To get most of my data back I had to open my original directory, 
which has a size of 122 MB and contains about 350 tables with 
5000 to 10,000 rows each.

Question 2:
Why does it take S-Plus more than two hours (!) to open,  i.e. to

(I know these are lots of tables but I have a fast machine)

Thank you in advance for your help.

messages.body_plain:
Myrtille Vivien asks:

> 
> may be it is obvious, but I don't see the solution :
> 
> In a program I do :
> 
> .
> .
> PK<-list(NULL)
> proj<-function(x,D)as.matrix(x)%*%MP(t(x)%*%D%*%x)%*%
> t(as.matrix(x))%*%D
> browser()
> PK<-lapply(1:ntabX,function(i,X,D)proj(as.matrix(X[,i
> ]),D),X=Tk[[kin]],D=D)
> .
> .
> .
> where :
> D is a matrix n *n
> Tk[[kin]] is a matrix n*ntabX
> MP is a function to calculate the Moore penrose
> Inverse
> 
> When I test my program with data, this error occurs :
> 
> Problem: "1:ntabX" is not a function
> 
> Why does lapply need a function here ??????!?????
> 
> When I make these operations out of my program, it's
> ok .

Four quick points that go to a more general problem than we have here.

1. What you have given is an extract from the story sufficient to
explain your own dilemma, but probably not sufficient to enable anyone
else to see what the real problem is.  You are in all likelihood
looking in the wrong place (and yes, I did notice you have a call to
browser() in there).  Certainly I can't see how you could have got
such a message, but if someone else can, then I withdraw my comment. 

2. You don't say what version of S-PLUS you are using.  I would guess
that it is S-PLUS 5.0 for Solaris, but I'm not prepared to bet.  This
might well be pertinent information.

3. If this is the calculation you wish to do you are going about it in
a needlessly complicated way.  These are, after all, just a series of
rank 1 oblique projector matrices.  In fact such explicit matrices are
so rarely needed explicitly I would wonder if you really need to
calculate them at all.  Ggenerally speaking it is only the operation
of projection that is needed and that can be done in many other,
simpler ways than by matrix multiplication. The act of simplifying and
streamlining the algorithm and code itself is often enough to remove
many obscure bugs: it is not necessarily wasted time.

4. In trying to find bugs, a neat layout definitely makes things
easier.  As far as I can see your code above does not have one space
in it and it reads like some unintelligible cypher.  (If your space
key is broken it might not be a bad idea to fix it!)  There are many
unnecessary things in it, too, like most of the as.matrix() calls.  My
advice is to pare it down to the proven essentials and no more.

-- 
Bill Venables,      Statistician,     CMIS Environmetrics Project
CSIRO Marine Labs, PO Box 120, Cleveland, Qld,  AUSTRALIA.   4163
Tel: +61 7 3826 7251           Email: Bill.Venables at cmis.csiro.au    
Fax: +61 7 3826 7304      http://www.cmis.csiro.au/bill.venables/

messages.body_plain:
I was writing a function which builds up a list of list of dataframes
and came across the following peculiarity. 

Define the following two functions, 

f <- function() data.frame(a1=1:2, a2=c('1','2'))

g <- function() 
{
  x <- list()
  i <- 'A'
  x[[i]] <- list(a = f())
  x[[i]]$a <- f()

  print(x)
}

then call g(). On our Splus 3.4 for Solaris this dumps core with a 'bad address'
error. 
        It seems to be important that f returns a dataframe that contains a
factor. It also seems to be important that the subscripting occurs in a function
(g in this case). The print will work if it is taken out of the function and
done from the command line. Is this a bug or am I missing something obvious?

        Matt

> Subject: [S] Subsetting with is.element or match
>

> Well I thought I had this under control, but the mystery of
> Splus almost
> corrupted my data base.
>
> Let me set up the problem.  I have two data objects
> > dim(large.object)
>  [1] 78413 5
>
> > dim(small.object)
> [1] 76118  3
>
> The two objects have an identical attribute, and I need to find which
> ones they are and use only those common ones in future analysis.
> However,  as you can see from the differences in the size of the data
> frames there is not a 1:1 correspondence between them.
>
> It was suggested that I use "is.element" or  "match"  to subset the
> larger frame selecting only the elements common to both data objects.
>
> I used the following command in a script file:
>
> test.frame <- big.frame[is.element(big.frame$zone , small.frame$zone)]
>   ### where zone is the attribute used to find common between the data
> objects
>  ### I can substitute "match" for "is.element"  here and produce the
> same result.
>
> This creates a data object which is the problem.
> > dim(test.frame)
> [1 ] 78413  78373
>
> I thought that this should have simply returned an object that was
> smaller that the dim of large.frame as defined  above.  What is
> happening, and what am I doing wrong?
>

You missed out an important comma! This should work:

test.frame <- big.frame[is.element(big.frame$zone , small.frame$zone), ]

BTW match and is.element are not synonymous. Each are called like this:

> is.element(Set, Table)
> match(Set, Table)

where you want to match elements in Set with elements in Table. Both calls
return a vector of the same length as Set. BUT is.element returns a logical
saying whether the element has a match in Table, whereas match returns the
index of the matching element in Table, and by default NA if no match.
Subsetting on these is completely different. For example

> Table <- 2:3
> Set <- 1:3
> is.element(Set, Table)
[1] F T T
> Set[is.element(Set, Table)]
[1] 2 3
> match(Set, Table)
[1] NA  1  2
> Table[match(Set, Table)]
[1] NA  2  3
> match(Set, Table, nomatch = 0)
[1] 0 1 2
> Table[match(Set, Table, nomatch = 0)]
[1] 2 3

With is.element you subset on Set; with match you subset on Table.

By the way, is.element is defined in terms of match:

> is.element
function(el, set)
!is.na(match(el, set, nomatch = NA))

messages.subject_clean: [S] function to return week number from a date variable?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Michale,

S+ has a function called 'yeardays', which returns the day number in the
year.  It would therefore be natural to expect the function you is looking
for to be called 'yearweeks'.  However, this function does not exists and
there don't seem to be any other function doing what you want (I might be
wrong about this).  You can generate the week number for one full year at
a time using, e.g. for 1999 (0 means week 52 of the year 1998):

  cumsum(weekdays(seq.dates(from="01/01/1999", 
                            to="12/31/1999", 
                            by="days")) == "Mon")

Assuming you want weeks to start on monday.  Based on this a
function 'yearweeks' can be build.

I use S-PLUS 5.1 for HP-UX.

Regards,
Henrik

Hi Janine,

In general using random effect models to fit unbalanced longitudinal data 
(i.e., with different number of times) could be a right choice. You have to 
specify just the cluster variable=the subject-specific variable and fit a 
random intercept model:

lme(fixed=y~x1+x2+...,random=~1,cluster=x0). (look at .hlp file for the 
others options of lme())

This is similar to fitting a gee model with gaussian error and correlation 
structure cov(Yi,Yj)=k for all (i,j).

The problem (*and this is my problem too*) could be when the individuals 
have been measured at different times and the number of times is small (2 or 
3). How can I adjust my model for this variable?:

-by putting it as an offset term?

- by considering it as a classical explanatory variable in the model?

Classical reference books (Hand&Crowder's or Diggle-Liang-Zeger) seem 
missing of this case. Am I wrong?

Any comment is coming?

messages.subject: Re: [S] R: repetead measures using lme
messages.body_plain:
A paper by Schwertman and Heilbrun presents a simple method for dealing
with some of the issues raised in your post. They assume that a growth
curve for each subject is piecewise linear with known and common (to all
subjects) break points. They  estimate the paramters and variances with a
linear model and use  the Geisser-Greenwood method to adjust the degrees of
freedom to estimate the variances of the paramters. I found this
approach useful for estimating growth curves for seals, given the available
data.

These models could be probably be fit using the lme and perhaps, even, some
of the assumptions relaxed. 

%D 1986
%T A successive differences method for growth curves with missing data and
random observation times
%A Schwertman, Neil C.
%A Heilbrun, Lance K.
%J Journal of the American Statistical Association
%V 81
%P 912-916
%K Regression;Repeated measures

messages.subject: [S] Command to project tree size
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-Plus users,

Hi!. I'm trying to project size increment of trees based on fitted multiple 
linear regression model.  My aim is to determine the size of individual 
after certain number of iteration. How can I determined the size of trees 
after 20 iteration or when the sum of sdi is greater than a ceratin value? 
I've tried using the repeat command, but so far no success.

What I've done is to repeat the same functions (see below), for a number of 
times. I guess there should a better way of doing this, particularly when 
it involved iteration for many times. Appreciate any response.

#       a is data file
#       b0, b1, b2 is the parameter estimates from fitted multiple linear 
regression
#       dbh (tree size) and sdi (stocking density) are predictor variables

a<-data.frame(b0,b1,b2,dbh,sdi)

out<-function(x)

{       di<-b0+b1*x$dbh+b2*x$sdi # size increment
        dbh<-di+x$dbh        #size including predicted size increment
        sdi<-(dbh/25.4)^2    #stocking density
        out<-data.frame(b0,b1,b2,dbh,sdi)
}
a1<-out(a)
a2<-out(a1)
a3<-out(a2)

messages.subject: [S] week number, 2
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Week numbers seem to  follow the rule that the week (Monday to Sunday) 
containing the first Thursday of a particular year counts as week # 1 of that 
year. Days prior to this week count as belonging to the last week of the 
previous year. This rule satisfies the condition that there are no partial 
weeks in a year, and that each day belongs to a unique week number, even if it 
counts as last years' week.

Has anyone an idea who might have been interested in such a rule to be adopted?

Regards

----Message d'origine-----
De: Bill Dunlap <bill at statsci.com>
A: Bill Venables <venables at acland.qld.cmis.CSIRO.AU>
Date: 05/07/00
Objet: Re: [S] an error in using lapply 

> Myrtille Vivien asks:
> > may be it is obvious, but I don't see the
solution :
> > 
> > In a program I do :
> > 
> > .
> > .
> > PK<-list(NULL)
> >
proj<-function(x,D)as.matrix(x)%*%MP(t(x)%*%D%*%x)%*%
> > t(as.matrix(x))%*%D
> > browser()
> >
PK<-lapply(1:ntabX,function(i,X,D)proj(as.matrix(X[,i
> > ]),D),X=Tk[[kin]],D=D)
> > 
> > When I test my program with data, this error
occurs :
> > 
> > Problem: "1:ntabX" is not a function 
> > 
> > Why does lapply need a function here ??????!?????

lapply's ordinary arguments are named "X" and "FUN"
and all others
are passed to FUN when it is called.  Your call of
the form
 lapply(1:ntabX, function(i,X,D)stuff(), X=Tk)
is interpreted as
 lapply(X=Tk, FUN=1:ntabX, function(i,X,D)stuff())
because the argument named X is taken to be lapply's
argument X
and the next argument, which is unnamed, is taken to
be the FUN
argument.  Avoid the problem by not using X or FUN as
the name
of an argument to FUN().  E.g.
 lapply(1:ntabX, function(i,x,D)stuff(), x=Tk)

Dear S-Plus users,

I suspect this is a frequently asked question, but after searching some
archives, and manuals, have not succeeded.  Any
help would be greatly appreciated.

I would like to allow the user to specify what element in list of results
(resultslist) to plot against another element in
the same list.  In my case

the results list includes,
> names(resultslist)
[1] "x"  "y1" "y2"   "y3"

where x is a matrix of 12 "explanatory variables."

What I would like to do, is to allow the user to decide which y's they would
like the scatter plots to be plotted against (y1, y2 or y3).
My failed attempt appears below.   I've tried some variations using "get",
"eval", "substitute", but nothing seems to work.
(not so surprising, b/c I dont quite understand how this aspect of Splus works).

Any advise on getting this right would be greatly appreciated.

cheers,
Kevin

======================================+
Kevin P. Brand, Sc.D
Research Associate
Dept. Epidemiology and Community Medicine
Faculty of Medicine
Univ. of Ottawa
Ottawa, Canada
---------------------------------------------------------------------

myplot <- function(results = resultslist, output = "y1")
{
     par(mfrow = c(4, 3))
     outparam <- results[names(results) == output]
     x <- results$x
     for(i in 1:ncol(x)) {
          plot(outparam, x[, i], ylab = dimnames(x)[[2]][i], xlab = output, log
= "x")
     }
}

messages.subject: [S] Summary: Do long names slow function execution?
messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary: Do long names slow function execution?
messages.body_plain:
Recently I asked:
I generally like to use LongDescriptiveNamesLikeThis for variables when I'm
programming.  Because s-plus is not compiled, would that slow execution of a
function (in a large simulation), compared to single-letter variable names?
Or does s-plus "tokenize" the names in some way that makes name length
irrelevant?

I received two replies:

AFAIK long names need (little) more time as S+ does no preprocessing
like byte code compilation, but the difference should be minimal.
However, I'm not an expert on the internals. -- Dr. Jens Oehlschlägel

I doubt that the difference would be measurable -- Alan Zaslavsky

Thanks very much to the two respondents.

Because I had in mind a very long simulation, one that might run for 24
hours on a fast Pentium, I would still like a more definitive answer.
I may have to experiment, but if anybody can answer from detailed
knowledge of the basic operation of s-plus, I'd like to hear that
answer.

Dave Parkhurst

                        return(md2)
                }
                attr(val1, "hessian") <- hess1(th0, th1)

messages.subject: [S] Summary: function evaluation w/ specified list element
messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary: function evaluation w/ specified list element
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Steve McKinney, Bert Gunter, Julian Taylor for their responses to my
earlier post.

Steve explained that my original attempt failed because

     outparam <- results[names(results) == output]

returns a list of one element long.  He shows one way to force this to work.

     outparam <- unlist(results[names(results) == output])

However, he and the others suggested better alternatives.  Three are listed
below along with my original post.

thanks to all for your instructive examples!
cheers,
Kevin

#First: Exploit list subscripting.

myplot <- function(results = resultslist, output = "y1")
{
     snip<>
     outparam <- results[[output]]
     snip<>
}

# Second: If you want to allow y1, y2, or y3 pointer to be entered as argument
without
# quotes.

myplot <- function(results = resultslist, output = y1) # note y1 w/out quotes
{
     snip<>
     output_deparse(substitute(output))
     outparam <- results[[output]]
     snip<>
}

# Third: Illustrate use of eval.

myplot <- function(results = resultslist, output = "y1")
{
     snip<>
     outparam <- eval(parse(text = paste("results$",output, sep ="")))
     snip<>
}

=========  ORIGINAL POST  =======
From: owner-int_snews at statsci.com [mailto:owner-int_snews at statsci.com]On
Behalf Of Kevin_Brand at hc-sc.gc.ca
Sent: Friday, July 07, 2000 6:02 PM
To: s-news at wubios.wustl.edu
Subject: [S] function evaluation w/ specified list element

Dear S-Plus users,

I suspect this is a frequently asked question, but after searching some
archives, and manuals, have not succeeded.  Any
help would be greatly appreciated.

I would like to allow the user to specify what element in list of results
(resultslist) to plot against another element in
the same list.  In my case

the results list includes,
> names(resultslist)
[1] "x"  "y1" "y2"   "y3"

where x is a matrix of 12 "explanatory variables."

What I would like to do, is to allow the user to decide which y's they
would
like the scatter plots to be plotted against (y1, y2 or y3).
My failed attempt appears below.   I've tried some variations using "get",
"eval", "substitute", but nothing seems to work.
(not so surprising, b/c I dont quite understand how this aspect of Splus
works).

Any advise on getting this right would be greatly appreciated.

cheers,
Kevin

myplot <- function(results = resultslist, output = "y1")
{
     par(mfrow = c(4, 3))
     outparam <- results[names(results) == output]
     x <- results$x
     for(i in 1:ncol(x)) {
          plot(outparam, x[, i], ylab = dimnames(x)[[2]][i], xlab = output)
     }
}

======================================+

Research Associate

Faculty of Medicine

messages.subject: [S] Linux, Win4Lin, and S-Plus 2000
messages.body_plain:
I have "seen the light" after converting to Windows 2000 to get
more reliability than Win 98 and finding that Win2K is
an unbelievably bloated operating system (requires about
70 MB of RAM to run and is not very fast).  So I'm thinking
about converting to Linux.  I have installed RedHat 6.2 and
Win4Lin (see www.trelos.com).  The Win4Lin install takes
a fair amount of work (3 steps including one to update your
Linux kernel and one to update Win4Lin as the CD they
supply is a bit out of date).  So far Win4Lin is running S+ 2000
very well.  Win4Lin has you install Win98 into a Linux
directory and boots Win98 very quickly into an X-window.

Some advice for those thinking about Linux:
- The operating system seems to be a real one, unlike Windows.
   An example of this is that if a MS Windows session croaks
   under Win4Lin the Windows errors are isolated and rebooting
   Windows does not affect the rest of your Linux session.
- The KDE desktop environment is pretty neat
- If you want to dual boot with Windows (which is not required
   by Win4Lin), it's best to have Windows in the first partition on
   the hard disk, in a FAT or FAT32 partition.
- Partition Magic and it's utility Boot Magic provide the easiest
   ways to create Linux partitions
- Downsides to Linux: adding accessory devices such as Zip Drives
   and dial-up networking capability is a REAL pain.  Setting up
   ordinary (Ethernet) networking is a breeze.  Only certain modems
   are supported for dial-up networking.
- Downside to Win4Lin: it does not support sound at present, and will
   not run many video action games.  But it runs MS Office, Quicken,
   S+ 2000 and a lot of other stuff.

--
Frank E Harrell Jr
Professor of Biostatistics and Statistics
Division of Biostatistics and Epidemiology
Department of Health Evaluation Sciences
University of Virginia School of Medicine

messages.subject: RE: [S] unable to create summary file
messages.body_plain:
Chuck Taylor from the S-PLUS QA team provided this response, which I'm
including here for the benefit of all the s-news folk:

S-PLUS 2000 uses the files __sum4.txt and __sum4i.txt in the _Data
directory for internal housekeeping.  Occasionally they get out of synch
with each other, and the above message is the usual result.  The
solution is to simply delete __sum4*.* from your _Data directory (using
Windows Explorer) and then restart S-PLUS.  The necessary files will be
created automatically.

Most causes of this problem have been fixed in previous versions.  The
most likely cause in the context of /BATCH processing is allowing two
different S-PLUS sessions to access the same _Data directory at the same
time (perhaps using the /MULTIPLEINSTANCES flag).  This could also
happen if different users accessed the directory at the same time over
your network.

Another thing to check is that the attached library directory is
writeable.

> Should I just ignore it?

No.  See above.

Chuck

messages.subject: [S] Splus EPS and Adobe Illustrator font behavior
messages.subject_clean: [S] Splus EPS and Adobe Illustrator font behavior
messages.body_plain:
I discovered this morning that

  1) encapsulated postscript files created by Splus using Latin1 font 
encoding do not "correctly" import into Adobe Illustrator (US and 
Canada version).

  2) if they are created using "standard" font encoding, they do.

Details.

1) Latin1

You get latin1 encoding by using the command

  ps.options(setfont=ps.setfont.latin1)

With this specification, hyphens do not display or print when the 
file is imported into Illustrator. There undoubtedly are other 
differences...

The files do, however, print correctly when printed from the unix 
platform directly to a postscript printer.

2) standard

You get so-called standard encoding by using the command

  ps.options(setfont=ps.setfont.std)

With this specification, hyphens display and print when the file is 
imported into Illustrator. This is the Splus default.

This applies to Splus v5.x on unix, and probably earlier versions also.

I put "correctly" in quotes above, because this may be a 
North-American-only problem. Illustrator may very well be 
interpreting the file correctly for ISO Latin1 font definitions, and 
the American version does not conform to international standards. 
Also, this is the Macintosh version of Illustrator, and I believe 
Apple has its own unique font sets that are not ISO (and may pre-date 
the ISO spec). That is, the latin1 encoding for a hyphen is a 
non-printing character in the Apple font set.

-Don
--------------------------------
Don MacQueen
Environmental Protection Dept.
Livermore, CA, USA
Lawrence Livermore National Lab
--------------------------------

messages.subject: [S] survfit.coxph
messages.body_plain:
Paul Peng points out that the survival curve from a Cox model containing
an offset differs between Splus 2000 and Splus 5.1.
        survfit(coxph(Surv(futime, fustat) ~ age + offset(rx), ovarian))

 1. The SP 2000 answer is correct, that in 5.1 is wrong.             
The survival code's test suite had a test for a Cox model with an offset, but
none for the survival curve from a Cox model containing both an offset and a 
covariate.  (It has one as of today, though!)

2. The SP 2000 answer agrees with Splus 3.4, and also with the latest 
survival code as found on the system here.  The local code will be reflected
in the next Splus release.  I'm not privy to when that will be, but based on
prior frequency I'd guess sometime later this year.

3. I hadn't specifically known of this bug or tried to fix it, but it seems
to have been repaired since survival5 was posted.  We've been cleaning up
some odds and ends, e.g., addition of as.double() to all arguments in .C
calls, and I'd guess that such was the root of this problem.  

        Terry Therneau

messages.subject: RE: [S] Subscripting problem (fwd)
messages.body_plain:
I recieved a few helpful replies to my question about a core 
dump involving subscripting. Thanks to Charles Berry, Alan Zaslavsky, and David
Smith. The most important response came from Dave who confirms that this is a
bug, and it is limited to Splus 3.4. The fix I employed (sorry Dave upgrading to
version 5 because of this seems just a bit too drastic to me) was to spread out
the assignment. So instead of:

        x[[i]]$a <- f()

I did

        tmp <- x[[i]]
        tmp$a <- f()
        x[[i]] <- tmp

This cured whatever was confusing the evaluator. 

        Matt

---------- Forwarded message ----------
Date: Thu, 6 Jul 2000 08:26:11 -0700
From: David M Smith <dsmith at statsci.com>
To: 'Matt Calder' <calder at phz.com>
Subject: RE: [S] Subscripting problem

Deat Matt,

I wasn't able to reproduce this problem on our Solaris machine:

> f <- function() data.frame(a1=1:2, a2=c('1','2'))
>
> g <- function()
+ {
+   x <- list()
+   i <- 'A'
+   x[[i]] <- list(a = f())
+   x[[i]]$a <- f()
+
+   print(x)
+ }
>
> g()
$A:
$A$a:
   a1  a2
1 "1" "1"
2 "2" "2"

$A:
$A$a:
Error in dim(X) <- c(n, length(X)/n): Length of data (3) doesn't match
product
        of dimensions (2)

I'm not sure where that error came from, and it only happened the first time
I called g().  It might possibly be the source of your crash.  The code
worked fine in S-PLUS 5 and S-PLUS 6.

In answer to your question: your code is valid, so this looks like a bug in
the S-PLUS 3.4 engine.  No upgrades to S-PLUS 3 are planned, so if this bug
is a big problem for you I suggest upgrading to S-PLUS 5.

Sincerely,
# David Smith

I am running S-Plus 4.0 Release 3 on a PC with Windows NT 4.0 
Service Pack 5. I try to use two copies of S-Plus, cause I have a

The second, a batch file with a different working library (s_proj) is

Why the second copy I start do not work? It doesn't depend on the

Now I have checked the switch /MULTIPLEINSTANCES, the result 
was satisfying. I made the following steps:

1) Start an interactive session of SPlus, without switch
2) Start a Batch-file, with switch --> this occupates 1 processor 
(50% cpu-time)

3) I start an interactive job in the session, which takes the other 
50% cpu-time (both jobs require something like 95%). All ok.

I doesn't check, if it's possible to do 2 interactive sessions or 2 
batch files - i think, the latter must be possible...

messages.subject_clean: [S] ESS 5.1.16 released, and JSM-2000 BOF meeting for ESS
messages.body_plain:
The following message is a courtesy copy of an article
that has been posted to comp.soft-sys.sas as well.

ESS 5.1.16 has been released. 

ESS (Emacs Speaks Statistics), is an integrated development
environment for statistical data analysis, programming, and literate
data analysis (using Noweb).  It works for Emacs 19.34 and later, and
provides a unified interface for:
        S languages (S, S-PLUS, R);
        SAS;
        Omegahat;
        XLispStat environments (XLispStat, ViSta, Arc)

New features:
- uses "customize" for customizing options
- SAS features cleaned up
- many, many bug fixes

In addition, we'd like to announce that there will be a BOF (birds of
a feather) session at the Joint Statistical Meetings this August in
Indianapolis.  At least two of the core developers should be there,
and this would be a fine time to learn about ESS, learn more about
ESS's features, look at how it behaves under Windows (maybe Linux, if
we can find a laptop), for SAS, S-PLUS, and R, and discuss with some
of the developers what features you would like to see in future
versions.

The BOF session is set for Monday, August 14th at 5:30 at the Hyatt in
Salon A.  We hope to see you there!

--

messages.subject_clean: [S] Parameterizing regression function formulas, storing AIC from stepAIC, StatServer questions
messages.body_plain:
> Good afternoon,
> 
I am new to the S-news list, and I am hopeful that someone will be able to
answer some of my questions.  My background is mostly in SAS, so I am
relatively new to S/S-PLUS.  If these questions are repeated by others, I
apologize.  I don't think you'll find these questions to be on the easy
side, however!  Thanks so much to anyone who can help with these questions!

Question 1:
> How does one go about parameterizing the right hand side of the formula
> for regression functions such as glm()?
>       
I am in a situation where we do not know what the right hand side of a
regression function will be when a given analytic is to be run.  Therefore,
I am doing the following:

>       -Data frame "SDF1" contains data to be used in the regression
> (independent and dependent variables).
>       -Data frame "SDF2" contains one column only.  This column is of
> character data type, and it indicates the names of each of the columns in
> SDF1 which are to be used as independent variables in the regression
> function.
>       -Data frame "SDF3" contains one column only.  This column is of
> character data type, and it indicates the names of each of the columns in
> SDF1 which are to be used as dependent variables for different regression
> function runs.
> 
> So, once I import SDF1, SDF2, and SDF3, I have all of the data we need
> along with the list of independent variables for each regression function,
> and a list of dependent variables which will be used for different
> regression function runs.  Next, I create a vector X which stores the
> values found in the column in data frame SDF2.  The result is that X
> contains a list of the columns in SDF1 which are to be used as the right
> hand side in the glm() call.
> 
> This is where the problem comes into play.  How do I take the vector X and
> create a string which can be used as the right hand side in the regression
> function?
> 
> For example,
> 
> Say X = "var1" "var2" "var3" (where var1, var2, and var3 are columns in
> SDF1).
> 
The DESIRED glm call looks like this:

> glmobj <- glm(formula = SDF3[[1]]/ST ~ var1+var2+var3, family =
> poisson(link = log), data = SDF1, 
>       na.action = na.exclude, control = list(epsilon = 0.0001, maxit= 50,
> trace = F))
> 
> How can we use X (or some other means) to get the right hand side to
> appear as "var1+var2+var3"?
> 
> --------------------------------------
Question 2:
> How does one store in a data frame or vector the AIC or Cp values at each
> step of a stepwise regression run?  Also, how does one create a data frame
> or vector containing the list of variables sequentially added to the model
> in a forward stepwise regression method?
> 
> Example:
> 
> Say the output from a stepwise regression run looks like this (note: I
> used stepAIC, but the same could be said of any stepwise regression
> routine):
>  
> ____________________________________________________
> *** Stepwise Fitting process ***
> Start:  AIC= 134.65 
>  YTRANS1 ~ 1 
> 
>        Df Deviance      AIC 
> + DIM1  1  21.1633  25.1633
> + DIM2  1  35.3252  39.3252
> + DIM3  1 124.8300 128.8300
> <none>    132.6455 134.6455
> 
> Step:  AIC= 25.16 
>  YTRANS1 ~ DIM1 
> 
>        Df Deviance      AIC 
> + DIM2  1  9.12302 15.12302
> <none>    21.16333 25.16333
> + DIM3  1 19.91281 25.91281
> 
> Step:  AIC= 15.12 
>  YTRANS1 ~ DIM1 + DIM2 
> 
>        Df Deviance      AIC 
> <none>    9.123022 15.12302
> + DIM3  1 9.112346 17.11235
> 
>       *** Chosen Fit ***
> 
> Call: glm(formula = YTRANS1 ~ DIM1 + DIM2, family = poisson(link = log),
> data
>        = SDF5, na.action = na.exclude, control = list(epsilon = 
>       0.0001, maxit = 50, trace = F))
> Deviance Residuals:
>        Min         1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
>  -2.194839 -0.5963645 0.359823 0.767594 1.005615
> 
> Coefficients:
>                  Value Std. Error   t value 
> (Intercept) 2.28466480 0.17302821 13.204002
>        DIM1 0.43882233 0.08634168  5.082393
>        DIM2 0.04026973 0.01166302  3.452771
> 
> (Dispersion Parameter for Poisson family taken to be 1 )
> 
>     Null Deviance: 132.6455 on 8 degrees of freedom
> 
> Residual Deviance: 9.123022 on 6 degrees of freedom
> 
> Number of Fisher Scoring Iterations: 3 
> 
>       *** Stepwise ANOVA ***
> Stepwise Model Path 
> Analysis of Deviance Table
> 
> Initial Model:
> YTRANS1 ~ 1
> 
> Final Model:
> YTRANS1 ~ DIM1 + DIM2
> 
> 
>     Step Df Deviance Resid. Df Resid. Dev      AIC 
> 1                            8   132.6455 134.6455
> 2 + DIM1  1 111.4821         7    21.1633  25.1633
> 3 + DIM2  1  12.0403         6     9.1230  15.1230
> _________________________________________________________________
> 
> In this case, I want to create a data frame that indicates the AIC values
> of the model at each step of the process, along with the variable that is
> added at each step.  This would look like this:
> 
> Data Frame:
>       Variable_added          AIC
>       NA                      134.6455
>       DIM1                    25.1633
>       DIM2                    15.1230
> 
> All of this information is in the ANOVA table above.  How can I get this
> information into a data frame such as the one here?
> --------------------------------------------------------------------------
> ---------------------------------------
> 
Question 3:
> Are there limits on the number of data tables that may be used as input
> and/or output to an analytic when using StatServer?
> 
> I have noticed that creating an analytic in StatServer limits you to no
> more than 3 input data tables and 3 output data tables.  I need to be able
> to have more than 3 output data tables from our analytic.  How can I go
> about doing that?
> 
> --------------------------------------------------------------------------
> ---------------------------------------
> 
Question 4:
> In StatServer or S-PLUS, how can one handle a variable number of
> input/output data tables?
> 
I have an analytic for which the number of input and output data tables is
unknown.  It is actually a parameterized number.  I may have 3 input data
tables (from an Oracle database) and 1-20 output data tables (to an Oracle
database).  How can I create the StatServer analytic so that an
parameterized number of input and output database tables can be
handled/created?

> --------------------------------------------------------------------------
> ---------------------------------------
> 
Thanks in advance for your responses.  They are much appreciated!

--Reid Gilliam

>

messages.subject: [S] lme and spatial variability
messages.body_plain:
Please reply to me, not to the list.

Dear splus-lme users,
I'm working with splus 2000 on a windows-based pc, trying to use lme
with geostatistical-like data, to fit a model as simple as:

y = \mu * u + s + \epsilon

where:
y is an n-dim response vector;
\mu is a fixed intercept effect, common to all n locations;
u is obviously a unit vector;
s is an n-dim vector of random intercepts, assumed to be incorrelated
and having common variance;
\epsilon is a spatially correlated random error component.

My lme model specification goes like this:

lme(fixed = y ~ 1, random = ~1 | loc, cor = spc)

where:
loc is a location counter;
spc is a corStruct object.

Finally a couple of questions:
(1) Am I right in interpreting the (Intercept) StdDev in the random
effect output as an estimate of the common standard deviation of the
elements of s?
(2) If so is the square of the Residual StdDev an estimate of the common
variance of the elements of \epsilon (the sill in geostatistical
terminology)?
(3) MAIN QUESTION: There should be no reason for including a nugget
effect in spc, as the latter variance component should be redundant with
the common variance of the elements of s. Nevertheless including a
nugget effect in corStruct proves to produce more plausible values of
the range and smoother predicted surfaces. What kind of interpretation
should I give to the random (Intercetp) StdDev then?
Thank you for the attention,
Alessio

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

sorry, yesterday I forgot to attach the answers.
Here they are:

Steve McKinney:
Do you really need the matrix inverse? If you are just trying to solve
systems of equations,
you don't have to compute the inverse.

>>From the help page for ginverse():
"Better yet, matrix inverses can usually be avoided, e.g. using solve(x,b)
instead of solve(x) %*% b and qr.coef(qr(x), y) instead of ginverse(t(x)
%*% x) %*% t(x) %*% y or ginverse(x) %*% y."

Which computed inverse is better is a complex question, the answer
depending on the situation at hand.  What you really want is XINVERSE %*%
X = I where I is the identity matrix, all ones down the diagonal and
zeroes elsewhere.
This is a clean issue theoretically, but on a computer the factors of
machine precision, rounding errors and so on make the issue complex with
different answers for different situations. 
Thus, on a computer, it is best to avoid inverses whenever possible.

Vadim Kutsyy:
solve and solve.matrix are the same (solve calls solve.matrix).

ginverse will give you general inverse for any matrixes, including
singulars.  As matrix is getting bigger, it is probably getting close to
singular.  In general ginverse is less prompt to round off errors, but it
depends on your applications.

Siwik, Thomas:
there is at least a third method to compute the inverse: via a
QR-decomposition (see help on solve.qr.Matrix). which the better  method
is depends on your task. if your matrix is singular you are left with
ginverse or QR, if not solve seems to be more accurate. in  my opinion QR
is best for nearly singular matrices and for solving  linear systems of
equations. but try to calc a matrix norm:
                               ||A*[Inv(A)*A-I]||
to compare the precision of various functions for the Moore-Penrose
inverse Inv(A).
please let me know more refined responses than mine (if not quoted to  the
list), since i am rather new on splus.

Thanks

messages.subject: [S] beware "booleans" in data frames
messages.body_plain:
Here's an interesting tidbit that many of you know,
but newbies (and rusty buckets like me) can get fooled.

Summary: 
        data.frame() converts booleans to factors by default.
        Therefore, beware of using "if( )".
        Use the "==" operator inside "if( )"
        to interpret the boolean-derived factor correctly.

Demonstration:
> tmp<-data.frame(b=c(F,T))
> tmp    
      b 
1 FALSE
2  TRUE
> if(tmp$b[1])cat("#1 is TRUE!?\n")     ###Incorrect!
#1 is TRUE!?
> if(tmp$b[1]==T)cat("#1 is TRUE!?\n")          ### "==" is smart.
NULL
> if(tmp$b[1]==F)cat("#1 is FALSE!\n")          ### Yes, "==" is smart.
#1 is FALSE!
> tmp$b2<-as.logical(tmp$b)             ### as.logical() isn't so smart.
> tmp
      b b2 
1 FALSE  T
2  TRUE  T
> codes(tmp$b)  #And here is the source of the trouble. tmp$b is a factor,
not boolean.
[1] 1 2

The printing of "FALSE" instead of "F" should be the tip-off.
(But sometimes S-plus documentation writes FALSE when it means F-- e.g. see
the help file for "is.factor()".)

messages.body_plain:
> From: "Day, Roger" <day at pci.upmc.edu>
> Here's an interesting tidbit that many of you know,
> but newbies (and rusty buckets like me) can get fooled.
> 
> Summary: 
>       data.frame() converts booleans to factors by default.
>       Therefore, beware of using "if( )".
>       Use the "==" operator inside "if( )"
>       to interpret the boolean-derived factor correctly.

data.frame() also converts character data into factors.  This behavior is good
if you are using the data frame as input to a modeling function, but can be
annoying if you are primarily using it as a device for handling mixed data
(so you can conveniently subset rows) but prefer the original representation.
You can prevent this conversion by wrapping the expressions for the columns
in I(), which preserves the original mode with the special class "AsIs"
attached.

> X_data.frame(first=letters,second=I(letters))
> mode(X$first)
[1] "numeric"
> class(X$first)
[1] "factor"
> mode(X$second)
[1] "character"
> class(X$second)
[1] "AsIs"

I ended up making a new dataframe with just 0's and 1's in place of
the factor variables so that I could tell at a glance whether the nls
output was reasonable a reasonable fit.  Is it possible to modify the

messages.body_plain:
On Fri, 14 Jul 2000, Nicole DePriest wrote:

> 
> I had tried using
> 
>          options(contrasts=c("contr.treatment","contr.poly"))
> 
> which made no difference in the output.
> 
> For instance, I tried the following:
> 
> tmp1 = factor(c("a","b","c","d"))
> options(contrasts=c("contr.treatment","contr.poly")
> tmp2 = factor(c("e","f","g","h"))
> codes(tmp1)
> codes(tmp2)

Um. codes() does not tell you the coding, it creates a new one.
It is usually far too confusing to use it for an unordered factor.

as.numeric(tmp1) will give the codes used for both ordered and unordered
factors.  I would just forget that codes() exists!

> They both have 1, 2, 3, 4 as their coding.  I guess I don't completely
> understand what that contrast option actually does.  All I know is that
> using  "contr.treatment" whenever I  use lm, I get the expected
> output.  All I can ascertain is that this contrast option affects only
> functions utilizing strictly linear models, such as lm() or aov().

Not quite.  The contrasts are used whenever model.matrix is called, to
create a design matrix.  This is used by lm (and aov is a wrapper for lm)
and glm, but also for some non-linear models too (like ppr and nnet).

The following may help

> tmp1 = factor(c("a","b","c","d"))
> contrasts(tmp1)
  [,1] [,2] [,3] 
a   -1   -1   -1
b    1   -1   -1
c    0    2   -1
d    0    0    3
> options(contrasts=c("contr.treatment","contr.poly"))
> tmp2 = factor(c("e","f","g","h"))
> contrasts(tmp2)
  f g h 
e 0 0 0
f 1 0 0
g 0 1 0
h 0 0 1

These constrast matrices are used to create columns in the design matrix
by model.matrix.  In each case three columns are created for the main
effect, by including for each row the appropriate row of the above matrix.

--

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

For a logit regression,
the partial residuals for variable x(j) are so defined :

r(i,j) = x(i,j) *beta(j)    + working_residuals(i)

with :
beta(j) : estimated coefficient  for variable j
x(i,j) : ith observation for variable j

in S+ jargon,  the r(i,j) is computed with
(I suppose we have an object called  pic.glm):

predict(pic.glm, type="terms") + pic.glm$residuals

For each j variable, 
these i values  give (plotted against x(i) ) 
one residual plot

No problem for the term working_residuals(i).

But I do not understand how are obtained the terms
x(i,j)*beta(j) :

predict(pic.glm, type="terms")
returns j columns (OK :) )  . For each column j, the
ith value corresponds to x(i, j)) *beta(j) only up to a constant
(one different constant per variable/column)

a1)

Probably related question :

"

messages.subject: Re: [S] logit regression: partial residual plot
messages.body_plain:
The plot that you seem to describe is a component plus residual
plot, which one can get with plot.gam(.., residuals=T)

With non-normal errors there are major issues in deciding
what residuals it may be appropriate to use.

Consider:
  kyph.glm<-glm(Kyphosis~Age+Number+Start,data=kyphosis)  
  kyph.terms <- predict(kyph.glm,type="terms",family=binomial)
Here kyph.terms is a matrix (one column per term).  Each column
is centered, i.e. it has a mean of zero.

If you print out kyph.terms you will get, at the end
  attr(, "constant"):
  [1] 1.21

  predict(kyph.glm) 
gives the same result as 
  attr(kyph.terms,"constant")+apply(kyph.terms,1,sum)

Here "absent" is 1 and "present" is 2.

John Maindonald.

messages.subject: [S] Inserting NAs into vectors
messages.body_plain:
S-News readers,

One of the nice things about using the na.exclude option for the
na.action argument of lm() and glm() is that the fitted() function will
pad the fitted values vector with NAs as placeholders for the missing
values.  Unfortunately, the method that fitted() and resid() uses for
gls objects, created using the NLME library, does not pad the vectors
with NAs.  I know that Jose' Pinheiro is aware of this problem, and he
told me that he's working on the problem.  In the mean time, though, I

messages.subject: Re: [S] Inserting NAs into vectors
messages.body_plain:
On Mon, 17 Jul 2000, Paul Schwarz wrote:

> 
> S-News readers,
> 
> One of the nice things about using the na.exclude option for the
> na.action argument of lm() and glm() is that the fitted() function will
> pad the fitted values vector with NAs as placeholders for the missing
> values.  Unfortunately, the method that fitted() and resid() uses for
> gls objects, created using the NLME library, does not pad the vectors
> with NAs.  I know that Jose' Pinheiro is aware of this problem, and he
> told me that he's working on the problem.  In the mean time, though, I
> have been manually adding the NAs back in the vectors.  I was wondering
> whether others have been plagued by this problem and have devised any
> nice workarounds for it?

Well, not plagued.  But there is a simple workaround you can see in
predict.ppr in library MASS, which is to create a vector/matrix of NAs, and
then fill those rows indexed by the names/rownames of the objects you get
from the fitting function with na.omit.

So far na.exclude is only in S-PLUS 2000, and in no Unix version of
S-PLUS AFAIK, which makes its use pretty non-portable,

--

messages.subject: Re: [S] 2_D density estimation in Splus
messages.body_plain:
zednikova at yahoo.com (Mirka Zednikova)
>I want to do 2-D density estimation in Splus. I see how
>to values for say, a Gaussian kernel density on a grid
>using the intensity() function or kern2d(). What I
>don't see is how  to get the values for points that
>aren't on the grid. Do I need to interpolate myself,
>or is there an easy way to do this in Splus?

You've found one of the weaknesses of the supposedly modern fast
algorithms for density estimation brought to us in `research' journals.

Download locfit (http://cm.bell-labs.com/stat/project/locfit/).
It uses a modeling interface (similar to loess etc) and your
points can be either given directly to locfit() through the
ev argument (recommended approach for either a small dataset or
small # of evaluation points), or through the predict() function
(uses interpolation methods, recommended for larger datasets).

--Catherine.

messages.subject: RE: [S] Parameterizing regression function formulas, sto
messages.body_plain:
Keith,

I did receive a couple responses to question 1 which were helpful.
To parameterize the equation I ended up doing the following:

rhsformula <- eval(parse(text =
paste("Yresponse","~",paste(dims,collapse="+")))[[1]]),

where rhsformula is my equation, Yresponse is my dependent variable, and
dims is a vector containing strings (characters).  Now, I can call stepAIC()
with rhsformula as follows:

stepAIC.obj <- menuStepAIC(object = glm.obj, formula.upper = rhsformula, 
        formula.lower = Yresponse ~ 1, direction = "forward", trace.p = F, 
        print.short.p = F, print.long.p = F, print.anova.p = F,
print.correlation.p = F)

I appreciate all who sent me a response!  Using eval and parse was the key.

I also received a helpful answer to question 2 from MathSoft
representatives:
As many of you already probably knew, you can create a data.frame with the
AIC values and variables included in each step of stepAIC() by using the
$anova convention:

a <- stepAIC.obj$anova$Step
b <- stepAIC.obj$anova$AIC
dataframe.name <- data.frame(a,b)

Thanks for that as well!

I have yet to receive answers about questions 3 and 4, but I'm not surprised
since they are StatServer questions for the most part.

Thanks again!
Reid Gilliam
Operations Research Analyst
GRCI, Inc.

messages.subject: [S] apply() and dataframes
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,
        Hope you can help.  I need to apply a function to all the rows of
a dataframe.  A sample of the dataframe is as follows:  

bodypart      location    activity     object  duration
Right.Hand      Patio   Repetitive      Table   2.00
Right.Hand      Patio   Constant        Table   2.00
Right.Hand      Patio   Repetitive      Table   2.00
Right.Hand      Patio   Constant        Table   1.00
Right.Hand      Patio   Constant        Nothing 2.00
Right.Hand      Patio   Constant        Head    2.00

where the top row contains the column names  and duration is in
seconds.  Essentially I need to expand those rows whose activity field is
"Repetitive" into alternating rows of the object for the row and
"Nothing" for the duration specified.  For instance, sample output for the
first row should be something like:

location     object      duration 
1    Patio    Table         0.5
2    Patio    Nothing       0.5
3    Patio    Table         0.5
4    Patio    Nothing       0.5

Rows whose activity field is "Constant" are not altered except for an
extraction of the desired fields.
 
What I would like to do is construct a new file with these expanded rows
(when "Repetitive" occurs) inserted into the "Constant" rows.  So I
thought I could construct a function that simply looks through each row,
conditionally expands the row, and then bind all the rows together in a
new frame.  The function I devised (expand.rep) is below.  While I could
loop through each row and update a the dataframe after each loop I wanted
to try to use something similar to apply().  It is my understanding that
apply() works specifically for arrays, matrices, and on numerical
data.  Functions related to apply() do not seem to work either.  

Can anyone give me suggestions to optimize the function or the use of an
apply-like function.  I am working with S-PLUS 2000 with WinNT.    

much appreciation
-RAC

expand.rep<-
function(filerow, contact.rate = 1, duration.fraction = 0.5)
{
        duration.per.object <- duration.fraction/contact.rate
        duration.per.nothing <- (1 - duration.fraction)/contact.rate
        if(filerow$activity == "Repetitive" && filerow$duration != 0 &&
        filerow$object != "Not_In_View") {
                location <- rep(filerow$location, 2 * filerow$duration *
                            contact.rate)
                object <- rep(c(filerow$object, "Nothing"),
                          filerow$duration * contact.rate)
                duration <- rep(c(duration.per.object,
                         duration.per.nothing), filerow$duration *
                          contact.rate)
                return(data.frame(location = location, object = object,
                      duration = duration))
        }
        else {
                return(data.frame(location = filerow$location, object =
                    filerow$object, duration = filerow$duration))
        }
}

Hi Stephen,

The conditional Likelihood is egual to partial likelihood in Cox model when 
the method to handle ties is 'exact' (the risk set would represent the 
matched set in the logistic model and the 'case' is the 'failure').

Well, so you can use:

coxph(Surv(dummy,response)~x1+x2+...+strata(stratum),method="exact")

where dummy could be rep(1,n), response is the response variable (0,1) and 
stratum is the matched-set variable.

messages.subject: [S] Summary: conditioning plots
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Patrick Connolly, Nick Ellis, Brian Ripley, and Max Kuhn for their
response to my post.

Basically, I used the subscripts option to solve the problem (Patrick, Nick, and
Brian).  Max gave some useful info about nlsList.  My solution is a modification
of Nick's solution, something similar to that on page 321 MASS2 (Brian).  I've
changed variable names from my original post.  Solution follows.

Jarrett

f.pv.plot <- function(data,list.nls)
{
  xyplot(gamma~distance | fsite, data=data,panel=
         function(x,y,subscripts,...,Fsite,List.nls){
           x.seq<-seq(0,max(x),0.1)
           panel.xyplot(x,y,...)
           parms<-List.nls[[Fsite[subscripts][1]]]
           if(!is.null(parms))
           panel.xyplot(x.seq,f.matern.vgram(x.seq,range=coef(parms)["range"],
                                     sill=coef(parms)["sill"],
                                     smooth=coef(parms)["smooth"],
                                     nugget=0.0144),type="l")
         },
         Fsite=data$fsite,List.nls=list.nls)
}

messages.subject: Re: [S] Logistic Regression
messages.body_plain:
> I am doing some work on Logistic regression and have a simple question.
> Given my classification results (I know this is a very crude measure of
> goodness-of-fit) how should I assess them?  In other words, what percentage
> represents a 'good' model - and what would give an 'excellent' model.  
> I know there is no solid answer to this - but I'd like to get a feel for how
> other people assess model quality.

You didn't give any specifics on your project, but I would offer a
general comment that if your objective is not in fact classification,
then accuracy of classification may not be a particularly relevant
criterion for the "goodness of fit" of the regression.  In particular,
don't assume just because some logistic regression programs give a
measure of percent accurately classified that you have to "do well" by
that measure.  For example, in a medical problem, we may have very little
prognostic power from available variables but if we can show that a 
particular treatment reduces probability of mortality by 5%, this is
very useful information even if we can't predict very well which patients
would have died.  In other cases, classification may indeed may be the
objective and then you are in a position to think about which assessment
measures best correspond to your needs, as suggested by Brian's message.

messages.subject: Re: [S] Logistic Regression
messages.body_plain:
Alan Zaslavsky wrote:
> 
> > I am doing some work on Logistic regression and have a simple question.
> > Given my classification results (I know this is a very crude measure of
> > goodness-of-fit) how should I assess them?  In other words, what percentage
> > represents a 'good' model - and what would give an 'excellent' model.
> > I know there is no solid answer to this - but I'd like to get a feel for how
> > other people assess model quality.
> 
> You didn't give any specifics on your project, but I would offer a
> general comment that if your objective is not in fact classification,
> then accuracy of classification may not be a particularly relevant
> criterion for the "goodness of fit" of the regression.  In particular,
> don't assume just because some logistic regression programs give a
> measure of percent accurately classified that you have to "do well" by
> that measure.  For example, in a medical problem, we may have very little
> prognostic power from available variables but if we can show that a
> particular treatment reduces probability of mortality by 5%, this is
> very useful information even if we can't predict very well which patients
> would have died.  In other cases, classification may indeed may be the
> objective and then you are in a position to think about which assessment
> measures best correspond to your needs, as suggested by Brian's message.
> -----------------------------------------------------------------------

> send e-mail to s-news-request at wubios.wustl.edu with the BODY of the

wanted to get some others' opinions.  Oftentimes I need to fit regression
models where my dependent variable is a rate.  For example:

Well, you would do better to look at methods, e.g. in Huber's book. rreg is
not using a recommended method, in that it chooses the scale by iterated
MA, and *that* is the problem.  Had its authors understood enough to follow
Huber's suggestions, you would have got a better result.  Can I suggest
that you use a more modern and competently implemented method, such as
lmRobMM or rlm in library(MASS)?

wonderful their implementation was!  Even at the time it was seriously

messages.subject: [S] Summary: Goodness Of Fit for mixture models?
messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary: Goodness Of Fit for mixture models?
messages.body_plain:
Last week I submitted a question to the list and to other contacts on how 
to test the GOF for mixture models.

Copies of the original post and the responses received are included below.

Thanks to Dr. Richard Olshen, Dr. Trevor Hastie, Doug Martin & Frank 
Lawrence for their help and input.

In my digging through references I found two that I think are very 
interesting for the GOF problem. Anyone interested in this question should 
put them in their "things-to-read" pile:

Mixture Models: Theory, Geometry and Applications; Bruce G. Lindsay, 
NSF-CBMS regional conference series in probability and statistics, Vol 5; 
Institute of Mathematical Statistics, Hayward CA, 1995.

Residual Diagnostics for Mixture Models; Bruce G. Lindsay & Kathryn Roeder, 
JASA, Sept 1992, Vol 87, No. 419, pg 785-794.

Thanks again to all.
John
]

----------------------------------------------------------------------------
ORIGINAL POST:

S-plus gurus:

I have been working on a mixture modeling project. We are modeling cell 
sensitivity to radiation using a mixture of 3 gammas. (We chose a 
3-component mixture because we are certain there are 3 different cell 
populations. N is about 300 cells.) I would like to include a 
goodness-of-fit test in our routine but have been unable to find a 
reference or appropriate technique. I reviewed Titterington, Everitt & Hand 
and V&R and searched the list...can't seem to find a solution. I thought 
about using a ChiSq approach using the fitted model to calculate the 
"expected" values and comparing with the actual data. Can anyone suggest a 
better way to test the GOF of such a model?

Thanks in advance to all.
John

----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Abstracted from comments by Dr. Olshen:

What you ask is tricky, for several reasons.  First, I believe that with
sufficiently many gammas and suitable mixing, you can approximate any
distribution on the position half-line in many senses.  Second, there are
eight parameters to your model if I count correctly:  two each for the
gamma components, and two for the mixing distribution (not three since the
sum of probabilities is 1).  That gives you much freedom and makes
issues of goodness of fit difficult unless you've much data.

Having said all that, here are a few suggestions.  First, take your fitted
model and simulate from it a sample the same size as what you have.  Fit
the parameters again.  You should come out with at least approximately
the same fit.  If not, a bad sign.  What's a good fit?  Well, you can
repeatedly take samples the same size and look at the spread, marginally
or jointly.  This amounts to a sort of "parametric bootstrap" approach.

.....

----------------------------------------------------------------------------
>From   Trevor Hastie   (hastie at stat.stanford.edu )

Your suggestion sounds fine. Break x up into intervals, compute
expected probabilities in the intervals, and compare with observed
via a Chi squared test.
Trevor

----------------------------------------------------------------------------
>From Doug Martin:

Another possibility (not necessarily "better") is to make a qq-plot based on
the quantiles of your fitted mixture model.  I have done this when fitting
normal mixtures, and found it to be a useful visual check.  Maybe
Atkinson's simulation envelopes could be used as well.

Doug

----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Some good ref's from Frank R. Lawrence:

I am very interested in mixture modeling.  I would appreciate it if you 
would let me know the responses to your posting.

For goodness of fit, I recommend the following references:

Hosmer, D.W.  (1978).  A use of mixtures of two normal distributions in a 
classification problem.  J. Statist. Comput. Simul., 6, 281-94.

Basford & McLachlan.  (1985). The mixture method of clustering applied to 
three-way data.  Journal of Classification, 2, 109-25.

Uebersax & Grove.  (1993).  A latent trait finite mixture model for the 
analysis of rating agreement.  Biometrics, 49, 823-35.

Muthen & Shedden (1999). Finite mixture modeling with mixture outcomes 
using the EM algorithm.  Biometrics, 55, 463-69.

Banfield & Raftery. (1993). Model-based Gaussian and non-Gaussian 
clustering.  Biometrics, 49, 803-21.

Verbeke & Lesaffre (1996). A linear mixed-effects model with heterogeneity 
in the random-effects population.  JASA, 91, 217-21.

http://www.stat.Washington.edu/fraley/

messages.subject: answers: [S] superscripts and trellis
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the following suggestions regarding my question:

> I would like to prepare some "publication quality" figures using
> trellis graphics using Splus Version 5.1 Release 1 for Sun SPARC. 
> 
> In particular, I would like to indicate units of measurement in the
> axis labels.  For example, density is measured in kilograms per cubic
> meter, so I would like to do something TeX-like:
> 
>         xlab = list("density (kg/m^3)",cex=1)
> 
> where "^" indicates superscript.  Of course, this doesn't work, but I
> was hoping someone might know what does work.
> 
> Another example is to label axis ticks on a map with degrees west,
> north, etc. using something like:
> 
>   scales = list(x=list(tick.number=8,
>                                 at=21+0:7,
>                             
> labels=c("","20^oW","","10^oW","","0","","210^oE"),
>                                    cex=0.5),
> 
> More generally, is there any way to gain access to the TeX fonts for
> Splus graphics?  They would be useful also for tick labels and for
> text.

What I have learned is that a LOT OF WORK is required if you really
want publication-quality graphics in Splus.  

I have decided to use the LaTeX psfrag package, which is a pain, but
it will more or less get the job done.  The idea is to insert a tag
with Splus where you want something better and let LaTeX import the
.eps file, find the tag, and repalce it with what you really want.
This requires downloading and installing psfrag from CTAN and then
preparing a LaTeX document that imports and corrects the .eps file and
creates a .dvi file, which dvips can convert into a .ps file.  Care is
needed, because not all tags work.  For example, I needed to take the
entire axis label as the tag, not just the bit I wanted to modify.
This changes the fonts, so the other axis (and possibly other figures)
should be modified.  Also, a lot of fooling around is needed to get
the size and position right.  Finally ps2epsi didn't successfully
convert the .ps file back to .eps.

I have not yet figured out how to get the Splus-only suggestions
working and I have already spent more time than I can justify.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. From Mike.Prager at noaa.gov:

I am tempted to label yours a PIQ -- Persistently Ignored Question.  At 
least, MathSoft has not responded so far to a chorus of requests for more 
flexibility using math and Greek in axis labels.

Several methods are used for this sort of thing, none of them very 
desirable, IMO.  I will sketch out what I know of them; I'm sure others, 
more knowledgeable than I, will fill in the details.

On Windows, one can use editable graphics, which support limited math 
expressions, then capture the commands generated by S-Plus and use them in 
future scripts.  I have found this to work well in some cases, but in 
others, the graph after exporting to EPS exhibits faulty spacing of the 
superscripts.

Several other solutions better suited to Unix have been put forth, mostly 
relying on other software, shell scripts, and/or patches to generated 
PostScript code.  What they have in common is that they apparently work for 
many users, but they seem to be operating-system and configuration 
specific.  If you can search the archives of this news group, you will find 
one supplied by Greg Snow MathSoft recently, and another approach by Alan 
Zaslovsky (whose name I may have spelled wrong).

Finally, R (a free implementation of an S-like language) provides use of 
math in figures.  This was not well documented last time I looked (several 
months ago), but may be by now, and I don't know if R includes Trellis 
graphics or not.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

2. From bje at lif.hi.is

If you are going to import files into LaTeX you should be able 
to use psfrags to replace axis labels with LaTeX-style labels.

You will need to declare \usepackage{psfrags} in your preamble.

A helpful URL is 

www.statslab.cam.ac.uk/~rrw1/Computing/latricks.html

Bjarki Eldon

3. From P.Connolly at hort.cri.nz

I don't know about TeX, but if you don't find it, you can use
something called mixed.text() which is designed to mix font faces,
sizes and vertical placing.  It is somewhat clumsy to use it with
Trellis.  One has to do a mtext type of operation.  I can tell you how
to go about it if you don't find TeX methods.  If you do, I'd like to
know about it.

best

-----Original Message-----
From: Alan Zaslavsky [mailto:zaslavsk at hcp.med.harvard.edu]

This is a definite FAQ - shows up about once every year.  Here are several
solutions:

(1) for a single Greek character: use the "symbol" font (Font 13 on Unix
systems, I don't know about the PCs).

(2) if it suits your needs and you are on a PC, use the graph editing
features.

(3) if you need to mix things up in one label, use my "postscriptfonts"
archive from Statlib. THese functions allow you to create simple to
moderately complex labels using a string with escape sequences for change
of font, super and subscripts, change of size, etc.  Takes some fiddling
to make it beautiful but it works entirely within S-plus.

(4) use the "psfrag" utilities (there are a few variations around) that
work with LaTeX or TeX, so you can create the label in those languages and
have them appear within a PostScript plot.  THe way to go for truly
high-quality typesettnig, but requires some additional steps.

Carlisle--you can install the attached functions supsub and msupsub,

Let me know if a piece is missing.  This version uses a generic set of

the font metrics are different in motif() or openlook() vs. postscript,
best do this adjustment using postscript output.

stringwid<-function(string, pointsize = ps.options()$pointsize, 
inches = T, cex = par("cex"), font = par("font"))
{
emdashes <- sum(afm.std[substring(string, 1:nchar(string), 1:nchar(
                string))])
        on.exit(par(old.par))
        old.par <- par(cex = cex, font = font)
        (emdashes * par("cin")[2])/1.2  #(emdashes * par("cin")[2])
}
#=============================================================
mix.text<-function(x, y, font, texts, offset = rep(0, nfont), 
 raise = rep(0, nfont), cex = rep(1, nfont), srt = 0, slope, 
noprint = F, col = 1)
{
        if(noprint)
                text <- function(...)
                NULL
        if(length(x) != 1 || length(y) != 1)
                stop("must give single x,y values")
        nfont <- length(font)
        if(nfont != length(texts))
                stop("must give same number of fonts as texts")
        if(length(raise) != nfont)
                stop("if given, raise must same same length as fonts")
        if(length(cex) != nfont)
                stop("if given, cex must same same length as fonts")
        if(length(col) != nfont) {
                col <- rep(col, ceiling(nfont/length(col)))
        }
        raise <- raise * stringwid("m", 1)
        if(length(offset) == 1)
                offset <- c(offset, rep(0, nfont - 1))
        else if(length(offset) != nfont)
                stop("must have 1 offset or as many as fonts")
        offset <- offset * stringwid("m", 1)
        uin.x <- par("uin")[1]
        uin.y <- par("uin")[2]
        cex <- cex * par("cex")
        if(!missing(slope)) {
                if(!missing(srt))
                        stop("only one of srt or slope may be given")
                else srt <- (180/pi) * atan((slope * uin.y)/uin.x)
        }
        trans <- 0      ### translation along axis of text
        srt.cos <- cos((srt * pi)/180)
        srt.sin <- sin((srt * pi)/180)
        for(i in seq(font)) {
                trans <- trans + offset[i]
                text(x + (srt.cos * trans - srt.sin * raise[i])/uin.x, y + (
                        srt.sin * trans + srt.cos * raise[i])/uin.y, texts[i],
                        font = font[i], adj = 0, cex = cex[i], srt = srt, col
                         = col[i])
                trans <- trans + stringwid(texts[i], font = font[i], cex = 
                        cex[i])
        }
}

                if((xside && old.axt$xaxt == "l") || (!xside && old.axt$yaxt == 
                        "l")) {
                        at <- log10(at)
                }
        }
        if(missing(srt))
                srt <- ifelse(xside, 0, 90)
        x <- switch(side,
                at,
                par("usr")[1] - old.cex * par("1em")[1] * (line + 1),
                at,
                par("usr")[2] + old.cex * par("1em")[1] * (line + 1))
        y <- switch(side,
                par("usr")[3] - old.cex * par("1em")[2] * (line + 1),
                at,
                par("usr")[4] + old.cex * par("1em")[2] * (line + 1),
                at)
        nfont <- length(font)
        invisible(mix.text(x, y, font, texts, offset, raise, cex = cex, srt
                 = srt, col = col))
}
#===============================================================
supsub<-function(x, y, text, cex = 1, offset =  - length(nt)/1.8, font = rep(1, 
        length(nt)), col = 1, subchar = "_", supchar = "^", rscale = cex)
{
#Function plots subscripts and superscripts using zaslavsky's mix.text()
#designates "_" / "^" as escape characters indicating sub/super-scripts
        cm <- charmatch(text, c(subchar, supchar), nomatch = 0) 
        #FLAGS for sbu/sup 1=subscr,2= superscr
        nt <- text[!as.logical(cm)]     #retains all non-flag text
        raise <- rep(0, length(nt))
        cx <- rep(1, length(nt))
        shift <- cumsum(as.logical(cm))
        zip <- seq(along = cm)
        newindex <- zip - shift #running index for non-flag text
        specials <- newindex[zip[as.logical(cm)] + 1]   
        #index for chars sub/super
        raise[specials] <- (cm[cm > 0] - 1.5) * rscale
        cx[specials] <- 0.7
        mix.text(x, y, font = font, texts = nt, offset = offset, raise = 
                raise, cex = cx * cex, col = col)
}
#===============================================================
msupsub<-function(side = 1, text, cex = 1, line = 3, offset =  - emdashes/2, 
outer = F,
        font = rep(1, length(nt)), col = 1, rscale = cex, subchar = "_", 
        supchar = "^")
{
        cm <- charmatch(text, c(subchar, supchar), nomatch = 0)
        nt <- text[!as.logical(cm)]     #all non-flag characters
        raise <- rep(0, length(nt))
        cx <- rep(1, length(nt))
        zip <- seq(along = cm)
        index <- zip - cumsum(as.logical(cm))
        specials <- index[zip[as.logical(cm)] + 1]
        raise[specials] <- (cm[cm > 0] - 1.5) * rscale
        cx[specials] <- 0.7
        emdashes <- 0
        for(j in seq(along = nt)) {
#find stringlength for centering
                emdashes <- emdashes + sum(afm.std[substring(nt[j], 1:nchar(
                        nt[j]), 1:nchar(nt[j]))]) * cx[j]
        }
        mix.mtext(side = side, line = line, font = font, texts = nt, offset
                 = offset, raise = raise, cex = cx * cex, col = col)
}
#===============================================================
LEGND<-function(x, y, legend, lty = NULL, pch = NULL, cex = par("cex"), col = 
rep(1, 
        length(legend)), text.colors = T, fonts = rep(1, length(legend)), lwd
         = rep(2, length(legend)))
{
#legend plotted in colors, lines and points overlaid; pch treated as characters 
or numbers
#points omitted if < 0 or "NULL"
#note you must provide afm.std the default font metric vector
##gives only approximate layout for particular fonts
##x and y, UL corner or, if vectors of lenght 2, UL and LR corners
        if(text.colors) col.text <- col else col.text <- rep(1, length(legend
                        ))
        if(dev.cur() == 1)
                stop("Device not open")
        specials <- is.list(legend)
        lleg <- length(legend)
        if((length(lty) != lleg & !is.null(lty)) | (length(pch) != lleg & !
                is.null(pch)))
                stop("lengths of legend, lty and pch must match or be NULL")
        cex1 <- cex/par("cex")
        char.height <- cex1 * par("cxy")[2]
        coords <- par("usr")
        linelength <- cex1 * 0.05 * (coords[2] - coords[1])
        if(length(x) == 1) {
#given ULH corner
                maxwidth <- 0
                for(j in seq(legend)) {
                        if(!specials)
                                maxwidth <- max(c(stringwid(legend[j]), 
                                  maxwidth))
                        else maxwidth <- max(c(stringwid(paste(legend[[j]], 
                                  collapse = "")), maxwidth))
                }
                boxwidth <- maxwidth/par("uin")[1] + 0.11 * (coords[2] - 
                        coords[1]) * cex1
                boxheight <- (1.3 * length(legend) + 0.3) * char.height
                lines(c(x, x, x + boxwidth, x + boxwidth, x), c(y, y - 
                        boxheight, y - boxheight, y, y))
        }
        else {
#give UL & LR corners
                boxwidth <- x[2] - x[1]
                boxheight <- y[1] - y[2]
                x <- x[1]
                y <- y[1]
                lines(c(x, x, x + boxwidth, x + boxwidth, x), c(y, y - 
                        boxheight, y - boxheight, y, y))
        }
        for(j in seq(legend)) {
                if(!is.null(pch)) {
                        if(is.character(pch) & pch[j] != "NULL")
                                points(x + 0.015 * cex1 * (coords[2] - coords[
                                  1]) + 0.5 * linelength, y - (j - 1) * 
                                  char.height * 1.3 - 0.65 * char.height, pch
                                   = pch[j], cex = cex, col = col[j])
                        if(is.numeric(pch) & pch[j] >= 0)
                                points(x + 0.015 * cex1 * (coords[2] - coords[
                                  1]) + 0.5 * linelength, y - (j - 1) * 
                                  char.height * 1.3 - 0.65 * char.height, pch
                                   = pch[j], cex = cex, col = col[j])
                }
                if(!is.null(lty))
                        if(lty[j] >= 0)
                                lines(c(x + 0.015 * cex1 * (coords[2] - 
                                  coords[1]), x + 0.015 * cex1 * (coords[2] - 
                                  coords[1]) + linelength), rep(y - (j - 1) * 
                                  char.height * 1.3 - 0.65 * char.height, 2), 
                                  lty = lty[j], col = col[j], lwd = lwd[j])
                if(!specials) {
                        text(x + 0.1 * (coords[2] - coords[1]) * cex1, y - (j -
                                1) * char.height * 1.3 - 0.65 * char.height, 
                                legend[j], adj = 0, font = fonts[j], cex = 
                                cex, col = col[j])
                }
                else {
                        supsub(x + 0.1 * (coords[2] - coords[1]) * cex1, y - (
                                j - 1) * char.height * 1.3 - 0.65 * 
                                char.height, legend[[j]], offset = 0, cex = 
                                cex, col = col[j])
                }
        }
        NULL
}

messages.subject: [S] Executing scripts from command window
messages.body_plain:
My thanks to Steve McKinney, Nicole DePriest, Andreas Krause and
Rob Balshaw:

Andreas Krause identified the problem:
I assume you declare a function in your script and then run it.
If that's the case, the command line can't possibly know of any
changed
parts of the function unless you declare it again. If you save
it, it is saved
to the external file but not declared to Splus.

Rob Balshaw :
You must "execute" the new definition after every edit in order
that S-PLUS know about the editing.
Otherwise, it must use the latest "executed" version -- that's
the one that it knows.

Steve McKinney from Mathsoft pointed out that you must 'source'
the script particularly in light of the fact that you can save
the script to disk more than once i.e. end up having multiple
versions:
Are you sure you ran (i.e. sourced) the modified script from the
script window (click the black triangle or choose Script - Run
from the menu) before executing it in the command window?

I was calling the function from the command line but not
'running' it first.  This is what caused the loss of
synchronization between the latest version of my function and
what was actually executing.

Nicole DePriest suggested the synchronize request.  According to
the help files this request is useful in long iterative
computations or where you suspect that a process outside of
Splushas affected your objects.

I will make sure to always run the script first (the black
triangle etc)

Alastair Dempster

Original question:
>When I try to execute a script from the command window, it is
the
>last version in memory that is executed.  So if I have made any
>changes to the script via the script window, Splus does not
>recognize them (and I have saved the script!).  What I end up
>having to do is run the script in the script editor window
>first.  Then when I execute it from the command window, I get
the
>correct version (ie. with the changes).

>How can I get Splus to execute the last saved version when I use

>the command window?

rmail has
