messages.subject: [S] S and efficient frontiers?
messages.body_plain:
Dear people of S-news

I'd most appreciate some advice on the following please.  I'm interested in 
the mathematical aspects of portfolio theory. I'm attempting to write S code 
to generate the efficient frontier

from a sample of funds from which I have return data.

For those not familiar with the Markowitz (risk-return) space and portfolio 
theory - the problem is as follows:

We have, say, 10 funds.  The proportion of capital I invest in each fund is 
described by the vector X. The elements in X have to sum to 1 obviously. We 
also have a vector of average returns from each of

these 10 funds (from a prespecified time period) and the variance-covariance 
matrix (say, Omega).

The efficient frontier is to be found at

max(X'%*%R - lambda%*%X'%*%Omega%*%X)

where lambda=(1/risk tolerance) = the slope of the efficient frontier.  
Lambda varies from inf to 0.

Our task is to solve for X for given values of R,Omega and lambda.  I have 
managed to generate the efficient frontier via brute-force numerical methods 
- but this takes too long (X is often of length 100 or more), and I'm hoping 
there is a better way to get at the

solution of the x's.

I recently purchased S-PLUS 2000 because I heard that it was a useful 
analytical tool that is frequently used in finance.  I would sincerely 
appreciate some advice on how others might tackle the problem, or whether 
there are suitable optimisers within S that can be used for this

purpose.  Alternatively, if anyone has tackled this problem previously, and 
has code they would not mind sharing, I'd love to have a closer look at it.

Thank you kindly.

D. Song

messages.subject: [S] Computational precision
messages.body_plain:
Hello everybody!

I've observed the following behavior which left me a bit startled.
(I'm using Splus Version 3.4 Release 1 for Sun SPARC, SunOS 5.3 : 1996.)

(Maybe this topic has been raised before; in this case accept my apologies
for the waste of bandwidth, but then I ask for references to (or subjects
of) respective mails on the archive. Thanks!)

An easy multiplication:

> 1/5 * 3/4
[1] 0.15

O.k., BUT then:

> 0.15 - 1/5 * 3/4
[1] -2.775558e-17

Can THIS be the result of lacking computational precision?
Does anybody have an explanation for this behavior and/or a workaround for
this?
Of course, one can use round() with a suitable number of digits to be
rounded to. In this case the following "precision" works:

> 0.15 - round(1/5 * 3/4, 16)
[1] 0
>  0.15 - round(1/5 * 3/4, 17)
[1] -2.775558e-17

However, I do not regard the computation from above as one where one
should expect any numerical problems.

Thanks for any hint.

 Regards  --  Gerrit

messages.subject: Re: [S] Computational precision
messages.body_plain:
?Gerrit Eichner <Gerrit.Eichner at math.uni-giessen.de> asks:
> An easy multiplication:
> 
> > 1/5 * 3/4
> [1] 0.15
> 
> O.k., BUT then:
> 
> > 0.15 - 1/5 * 3/4
> [1] -2.775558e-17
> 
> Can THIS be the result of lacking computational precision?
> Does anybody have an explanation for this behavior and/or a workaround for
> this?

Standard "floating point" representation used on almost computers expresses
numbers in the form (INTEGER) * 2^(INTEGER POWER).  Hence it does NOT
have an exact representation for fractions that are not multiples of a power
of 2.  So 3/4 = 3 * 2^(-2) has an exact representation, but 1/5 and
.15 do not.  Arithmetic with numbers that are not represented exactly
will not give exact results, something we most dramatically notice when
the exact result is 0.  Same issue applies to exact comparisons, e.g.

   > (1/5) * (3/4) == .15
   [1] F

There is no fully general way around this within the framework of
floating point.  You could do a little off-the-cuff numerical analysis and
figure out what degree of precision you can expect for a given
calculation (given that INTEGER is up to 17 decimal digits of
precision).

Some computer math packages have a numerical type for rational numbers,
which would guarantee exact results for your problem.  You could even
implement this in S reasonably easily, but I doubt that it would be of
much use for statistics.

messages.subject: RE: [S] S and efficient frontiers?
messages.body_plain:
I am currently writing a book on introductory financial econometrics and I
am using Splus to illustrate many of the computations. I am working on a set
of routines to do simple Markowitz efficient frontier stuff. For the case
with no restrictions on the portfolio weights (no short-sales restrictions
etc), I have no trouble computing an efficient frontier for an arbitrary set
of points. You need to use the fact that given any two points on the
frontier, all other points are
just linear combinations of the given two. Of course, with general
restrictions you have to result to more brute force methods although NUOPT
does this very fast. I hope to have some example s code up on my web site
(http://faculty.washington.edu/ezivot) later this summer together with a
tentative manuscript. ez

-----Original Message-----
From: owner-s-news at wubios.wustl.edu
[mailto:owner-s-news at wubios.wustl.edu]On Behalf Of CELLO SONG
Sent: Monday, July 24, 2000 8:11 AM
To: s-news at wubios.wustl.edu
Subject: [S] S and efficient frontiers?

Dear people of S-news

I'd most appreciate some advice on the following please.  I'm interested in
the mathematical aspects of portfolio theory. I'm attempting to write S code
to generate the efficient frontier
from a sample of funds from which I have return data.

For those not familiar with the Markowitz (risk-return) space and portfolio
theory - the problem is as follows:

We have, say, 10 funds.  The proportion of capital I invest in each fund is
described by the vector X. The elements in X have to sum to 1 obviously. We
also have a vector of average returns from each of
these 10 funds (from a prespecified time period) and the variance-covariance
matrix (say, Omega).

The efficient frontier is to be found at

max(X'%*%R - lambda%*%X'%*%Omega%*%X)
where lambda=(1/risk tolerance) = the slope of the efficient frontier.
Lambda varies from inf to 0.

Our task is to solve for X for given values of R,Omega and lambda.  I have
managed to generate the efficient frontier via brute-force numerical methods
- but this takes too long (X is often of length 100 or more), and I'm hoping
there is a better way to get at the
solution of the x's.

I recently purchased S-PLUS 2000 because I heard that it was a useful
analytical tool that is frequently used in finance.  I would sincerely
appreciate some advice on how others might tackle the problem, or whether
there are suitable optimisers within S that can be used for this
purpose.  Alternatively, if anyone has tackled this problem previously, and
has code they would not mind sharing, I'd love to have a closer look at it.

Thank you kindly.

D. Song

Four one-day short courses on statistical analysis with latent 
variables using Mplus will be held in Nottingham, United 
Kingdom, on September 5, 6, 7, and 8.

Nottingham, Division of Psychiatry, School of Community 
Health Sciences.  

These courses can be taken individually or in combination.  
Instructors are Bengt and Linda Muthen.

The four courses will cover introductory, intermediate, and 
advanced topics including exploratory and confirmatory factor 
analysis, general structural equation modeling, growth modeling, 
modeling with categorical outcomes, modeling with missing data, 
multilevel modeling, advanced growth modeling, and modeling 
with categorical latent variables including latent class analysis, 
growth mixture modeling, and analysis of randomized trials with 
noncompliance.  For each topic, issues of model specification,
identification, estimation, testing, and model modification will be
discussed. Modeling hints will be given. Mplus input setups will 
be featured and output will be used for interpretation of analysis 
results.

solve.

... , "seqtwenty".

each object, but
the first step in the FOR loop is to attach() the object in question.

object.
For example, this does not work:

object.list_c("seqone","seqtwo","seqthree")

for (n in 1:3)
{

    attach (object.list[n])

    # do some stuff with object

}

Dumped

for (n in objects(pattern="^seq[a-z]"))

I could perhaps construct an 'uber-object' which contains all the other

elegant

messages.subject: [S] Flavors of S
messages.body_plain:
I recently started using S-Plus 2000. After looking around a bit for a
reference to help me learn what I was doing, I found John Chambers'
"Programming with Data". The "corrected third primting" I have just came out
this year, so it seemed reasonable to assume that both the book and my
software were up-to-date; therefore things should be mostly compatible.

I was reading along, trying to get the examples to work, and nothing was
going right. From what I can tell, there are huge differences (at least
syntactic, if not conceptual) between S-Plus 5.1 and S-Plus 2000.

Given that, I was wondering if I could get some answers, or at least
opinions...

*Why were the changes so sudden, and so drastic?

*Why is 5.1 not available for Windows?

*Why is 2000 not availble for Unix?

*Is one or the other being phased out?

*In the near future (say 5 years), will most of the industry be using the
2000 syntax or 5.1 syntax?

*Which of these is the open-source language R closer to? (if the 5.1 line is
the way to go and R is closer to that than 2000 is, I may be better off
learning to use that)

Thanks in advance,
Chad Scherrer

messages.body_plain:
On Wed, 26 Jul 2000, Chad Scherrer wrote:

> I recently started using S-Plus 2000. After looking around a bit for a
> reference to help me learn what I was doing, I found John Chambers'
> "Programming with Data". The "corrected third primting" I have just came out
> this year, so it seemed reasonable to assume that both the book and my
> software were up-to-date; therefore things should be mostly compatible.

Reading just a little more carefully should have made that clear to you
(but Springer's publicity seems to shy aways from it).  See p.vi.
And when it says it `underlies S-Plus versions 5.0 or higher' it does
not mean that it describes them and there are marked differences.

S-PLUS 2000 is the marketing term for S-PLUS 4.7 (type
c(version$major, version$minor) for confirmation).

I'm very biased, but wonder how you hit on that reference not one of those
in the S-PLUS 2000 manuals. (And a quick check on Amazon.com shows
that a couple of others are many times more popular.)

> I was reading along, trying to get the examples to work, and nothing was
> going right. From what I can tell, there are huge differences (at least
> syntactic, if not conceptual) between S-Plus 5.1 and S-Plus 2000.
> 
> Given that, I was wondering if I could get some answers, or at least
> opinions...

Personal opinions follow. Hopefully Dave Smith will give an official view
from MathSoft.

> *Why were the changes so sudden, and so drastic?

Well, they were announced and discussed for several years, including at the
last two S-PLUS Users Conferences. And they are *nothing* like as drastic
as that book may make you think, as it only describes the `goodies' and
none of the old features (like graphics).

> *Why is 5.1 not available for Windows?

Because porting the new engine to Windows is decidedly non-trivial.
(Porting it to multiple Unix platforms was, too. Porting almost anything to
Windows is non-trivial in my experience, especially interactive things. Oh
for some serious standards compliance, and some Unix manufacturers should
be ashamed too, including those two MathSoft have dropped support for
recently.)  Windows users who want better tools should complain to
MathSoft to give out a certified POSIX subsystem.

> *Why is 2000 not availble for Unix?

Why would Unix people want it?  It has a slightly later version of the base
statistics code that 5.1, and a GUI that most Unix users of S hate in
principle or in practice. (The idea of a single-tasking GUI is a pretty
poor one, for example. And the GUI is non-optional if you want on-screen
graphics, unlike, say, R.)

> *Is one or the other being phased out?

S-PLUS 6.x^* for both Unix and Windows has been announced as being based on
the Svr4 engine, with no further development of the S-PLUS 3.x/4.x line.
(Now like the laws of the Medes and Persians, that is immutable until
circumstances dictate otherwise, I surmise.)

^* Some time Real Soon Now^(TM).

> *In the near future (say 5 years), will most of the industry be using the
> 2000 syntax or 5.1 syntax?

Many users are still using S-PLUS 3.3 from 1995 or 3.4 from 1996, including
me on Solaris.  See below for an eloboration.

> *Which of these is the open-source language R closer to? (if the 5.1 line is
> the way to go and R is closer to that than 2000 is, I may be better off
> learning to use that)

Currently, closest to 3.4 and hence closer to 2000 than 5.1.  But 
S-PLUS >=5 and R are both changing, R most rapidly.

However, I use all 3 S dialects regularly, and for most routine things the
old (3.x, 4.x) and new (5.x and later) S-PLUS engines are indistinguishable
with R more dissimilar.  It is only for serious S programmers that big
differences emerge, but those are Dr Chambers' intended audience (from the
back cover and p.vi). A trainee S programmer now should probably start with
5.x, but (s)he will need to know about many of the old things not in
Chambers (1998)

As (not just) a marketing plug, Bill Venables and I feel our `S
Programming' gives a much more balanced view of the merits of the different
S dialects (and as Dr Chambers' has feet in all camps, I am sure he would
not mind that comment: it was not his intention).

--

I have played around with the grep, regexpr, and paste functions and can't

values with underscores?

messages.subject: RE: [S] Flavors of S
messages.body_plain:
Perhaps it's worthwhile taking a few moments to explain the background here
for anyone who isn't aware of the relationship between S (a programming
language and environment) and S-PLUS (a software product from MathSoft which
includes an implementation of S).

"Programming with Data" -- also known as the Green Book -- describes S
version 4 (Sv4), the language designed and implemented by John Chambers and
team at Lucent Technologies.  Sv4 builds upon S version 3 in many ways, but
is largely backwards-compatible with Sv3.

MathSoft licences the S language and implementation from Lucent to create
S-PLUS.  The currently-released versions of S-PLUS for Unix and Windows are
based on different versions of S: S-PLUS 2000 for Windows is based on Sv3,
and S-PLUS 5 for Linux and Unix is based on Sv4.

S-PLUS 2000 for Windows is not based on Sv4, as it has taken some time for
the S-PLUS development team here in Seattle to port the Sv4 code from Lucent
to Windows and integrate it with the graphical user interface.  This is why
S-PLUS 5.1 is not available for Windows.  That work is now almost complete,
and S-PLUS 6 for Windows -- based on Sv4 -- will be released later this
year.  This brings both the Unix and Windows versions of S-PLUS onto the
same S language base, and all future versions of S-PLUS will be based on
Sv4.  Thus in the near future (much less than 5 years!) all S-PLUS users
will be using Sv4 (the 5.1 syntax).

The R language is closest to ("not unlike") Sv3; S-PLUS is the only
commercially supported platform for the S version 4 language described in
the Chambers book.

# David Smith

--

Are all of your first substrings the same length? If so, this is fairly
straightforward. In your example, they're all of length 9. Suppose "vec" is

paste (substring (vec, 1, 9), "_", substring (vec, 11, nchar(vec)), sep="")

plus the characters from 11 onward.

If you need to hunt through each of the strings for the separator character,
that's harder. You will, I suspect, need a loop for that.

messages.body_plain:
Here's a really crude version of an S-only solution.  A better version
would avoid sapply by vectorizing the whole thing, i.e. break out all
the strings in sss at once into characters, convert and then collapse
them back together in the right quantities.  Also it would do some 
more checking, etc. 

convert.char _ function(sss, old=".", new="_") 
{       ### sss = character vector
        ### old, new are characters to be translated
   convert.one _ function(ss, old, new) 
   {  
   n_nchar(ss)
   chars _ substring(ss, 1:n, 1:n)
   changed _ match(chars,old,0)
   chars[changed > 0] _ new[changed[changed>0]]
   paste(chars,collapse="")
   }
sss[] _ unlist(sapply(as.list(sss), convert.one, old=old, new=new))
sss
}

        ### example of use
> XX
[1] "asdfad.sdfd.asdfasd.asdf" "asd34.342.563.asdf..."   
> convert.char(XX)
[1] "asdfad_sdfd_asdfasd_asdf" "asd34_342_563_asdf___"   
> convert.char(XX,letters[1:4],LETTERS[1:4])
[1] "AsDfAD.sDfD.AsDfAsD.AsDf" "AsD34.342.563.AsDf..."

From: Biggerstaff, Brad J. [mailto:bkb5 at cdc.gov]

Subject: RE: [S] replacing substrings of character values

Try this (though not vectorized):

"replace.char"<-
function(x, char = " ",new.char="")
{
        x <- as.character(x)
        n <- nchar(x)
        chars <- substring(x, 1:n, 1:n)
        chars[chars == char] <- new.char
        paste(chars, sep = "", collapse = "")
}

Example:

> replace.char("ab.c.d",".","_")
[1] "ab_c_d"
>  replace.char("ab c",new=".")
[1] "ab.c"

brad

Ok, final recap:

I got excellent responses from so many people, it took me a while to try a
few things and find the easiest solution for me!  Again, I'm using S-PLUS
2000, so this may/may not work for some versions perhaps.

>>From Steve McKinney:

paste(unlist(unpaste(as.character("foo.bar.foobar"),sep=".")),collapse="_")
[1] "foo_bar_foobar"

This successfully converts the periods in the string to underscores.  I put
this in a for loop and got what I needed:

for (i in 1:nrow(dataframe_name)) {
dataframe_name[i,"column_name"] <-
paste(unlist(unpaste(as.character(dataframe_name[i,"column_name"]),sep="."))
,collapse="_")
}

This is excellent.  Other excellent solutions were given by Brad
Bigglesworth, Samuel Buttrey, Alan Zaslavsky, X Ju, and others.  Thanks for
the excellent responses!

- Reid

messages.subject: Re: [S] import.data without generating factors
messages.body_plain:
Thank you for responding to my question,
Tillmann Krahnke, Jean Adams, Trevor McMullan, and David Smith.

The correct incantation for import.data is
          StringsAsFactors = "Never"

It was also suggested that factors can easily be coerced into plain
character values, but it's not as straightforward as one might think (in
the context of data frames).
Here is an example (still Splus 2000 for Windows):

> xx <- data.frame(a=letters[1:4], b=11:14)
> xx
  a  b
1 a 11
2 b 12
3 c 13
4 d 14
> sapply(xx, is.factor)
 a b
 T F
> xx[, "a"] <- as.character(xx[, "a"])
> sapply(xx, is.factor)
 a b
 T F
# still factor!

generated filenames. For instance, the first file generated using a value of

fname <- paste(Plot.file, 'Plot###.', ExportType, sep = '')

           'User9', print.background = prt.back,

directory\Plot002.BMP, etc. as claimed by the help file;

directory\Plot900.BMP, directory\Plot100.BMP(this is not a typo, the first

> xx[, "a"] <- as.character(xx[, "a"]) feels compelled to recognise it's
> a part of a dataframe and to do what it does with dataframes.
> 
> It makes no difference if the xx[[ col.name]] approach is used.

> Is there a simple explanation?

[<- has a data.frame method and $<- does not, so x$a uses the method for
lists which does not promote character vars to factors whereas the
data.frame methods do.

Finally, the S-PLUS version is crucial here.  The original example works
in 5.1, as does A <- "a"; xx[[A]] <- as.character(xx[[A]])

--

messages.subject: Re: [S] detecting data precision
messages.body_plain:
Karen,

I think you can use the following trick. Convert your numeric vector to
character, count the number of digits following the point, if any. and
take the maximun of that.

a1 <- c(123, 1, 23.00002, 45)
tmp1 <- as.character(a1)
tmp2 <- regexpr("[.]",tmp1)
tmp3 <- ifelse(tmp2< 0, nchar(tmp1),tmp2)
max(nchar(substring(tmp1,tmp3+1,nchar(tmp1))))

By the way, this will result in 0 if a1 equals c(123, 45, 67) for
example.

Hope this helps,
Longhow

messages.subject: [S] obituary for John Tukey
messages.body_plain:
Though off normal topic boundaries, I thought this might be of interest to
the list.  

I believe it is fair to say that Professor Tukey had some importance
influence on S.

It appeared in the NY Times this morning.

The link is

http://www.nytimes.com/00/07/28/news/national/obit-j-tukey.html

and the actual text  (apologies for formatting flaws since I use a Microsoft
e-mail handler) is below.

Best Regards,
Bill
______________________________
Bill Pikounis, Ph.D.
   E-mail: v_bill_pikounis at merck.com
   Phone: 732.594.3913
   Fax:  732.594.1565

Merck Research Laboratories
P.O. Box 2000, MailDrop RY70-38
126 E. Lincoln Ave
Rahway, NJ 07065-0900

######## OBITUARY ################

John Tukey, 85, Statistician Who Coined 2
          Crucial Words

          By DAVID LEONHARDT

          John Wilder Tukey, one of the most influential statisticians of
the
          last 50 years and a wide-ranging thinker credited with inventing
          the word "software," died on Wednesday in New Brunswick, N.J.
          He was 85. 

          The cause was a heart attack after a short illness, said Phyllis
          Anscombe, his sister-in-law. 

          Mr. Tukey developed important theories about how to analyze data
          and compute series of numbers quickly. He spent decades as both a
          professor at Princeton University and a researcher at AT&T's Bell
          Laboratories, and his ideas continue to be a part of both doctoral
          statistics courses and high school math classes. In 1973,
President
          Richard M. Nixon awarded him the National Medal of Science. 

          But Mr. Tukey frequently ventured outside of the academy as well,
          working as a consultant to the government and corporations and
          taking part in social debates. 

          In the 1950's, he criticized Alfred C. Kinsey's research on sexual
          behavior. In the 1970's, he was chairman of a research committee
that
          warned that aerosol spray cans damaged the ozone layer. More
          recently, he recommended that the 1990 Census be adjusted by using
          statistical formulas in order to count poor urban residents whom
he
          believed it had missed. 

          "The best thing about being a statistician," Mr. Tukey once told a
          colleague, "is that you get to play in everyone's backyard." 

          An intense man who liked to argue and was fond of helping other
          researchers, Mr. Tukey was also an amateur linguist who made
          significant contributions to the language of modern times. In a
1958
          article in American Mathematical Monthly, he became the first
          person to define the programs on which electronic calculators ran,
          said Fred R. Shapiro, a librarian at Yale Law School who is
editing a
          book on the origin of terms. Three decades before the founding of
          Microsoft, Mr. Tukey saw that "software," as he called it, was
          gaining prominence. "Today," he wrote at the time, it is "at least
as
          important" as the " 'hardware' of tubes, transistors, wires, tapes
and
          the like." 

          Twelve years earlier, while working at Bell Laboratories, he had
          coined the term "bit," an abbreviation of "binary digit" that
described
          the 1's and 0's that are the basis of computer programs. 

          Both words caught on, to the chagrin of some computer scientists
          who saw Mr. Tukey as an outsider. "Not everyone was happy that
          he was naming things in their field," said Steven M. Schultz, a
          spokesman for Princeton. 

          Mr. Tukey had no immediate survivors. His wife of 48 years,
          Elizabeth Rapp Tukey, an antiques appraiser and preservation
          activist, died in 1998. 

          Mr. Tukey was born in 1915 in New Bedford, a fishing town on the
          southern coast of Massachusetts, and was the only child of Ralph
H.
          Tukey and Adah Tasker Tukey. His mother was the valedictorian of
          the class of 1898 at Bates College in Lewiston, Me., and her
closest
          competition was her eventual husband, who became the salutatorian.
          Classmates referred to them as the couple most likely to give
birth to
          a genius, said Marc G. Glass, a Bates spokesman. 

          The elder Mr. Tukey became a Latin teacher at New Bedford's high
          school, but, because of a rule barring spouses from teaching at
the
          school, Mrs. Tukey was a private tutor, Mrs. Anscombe said. Mrs.
          Tukey's main pupil became her son, who attended regular classes
          only for special subjects like French. "They were afraid that if
he
          went to school, he'd get lazy," said Howard Wainer, a friend and
          former student of John Tukey's. 

          In 1936, Mr. Tukey graduated from nearby Brown University with a
          bachelor's degree in chemistry, and in the next three years earned
          three graduate degrees, one in chemistry at Brown and two in
          mathematics at Princeton, where he would spend the rest of his
          career. At the age of 35, he became a full professor, and in 1965
he
          became the founding chairman of Princeton's statistics department.

          Mr. Tukey worked for the United States government during World
          War II. Friends said he did not discuss the details of his
projects, but
          Mrs. Anscombe said he helped design the U-2 spy plane. 

          In later years, much of his important work came in a field that
          statisticians call robust analysis, which allows researchers to
devise
          credible conclusions even when the data with which they are
          working are flawed. In 1970, Mr. Tukey published "Exploratory Data
          Analysis," which gave mathematicians new ways to analyze and
          present data clearly. 

          One of those tools, the stem-and-leaf display, continues to be
part of
          many high school curriculums. Using it, students arrange a series
of
          data points in a series of simple rows and columns and can then
          make judgments about what techniques, like calculating the average
          or median, would allow them to analyze the information
          intelligently. 

          That display was typical of Mr. Tukey's belief that
mathematicians,
          professional or amateur, should often start with their data and
then
          look for a theorem, rather than vice versa, said Mr. Wainer, who
is
          now the principal research scientist at the Educational Testing
          Service. 

          "He legitimized that, because he wasn't doing it because he wasn't
          good at math," Mr. Wainer said. "He was doing it because it was
the
          right thing to do." 

          Along with another scientist, James Cooley, Mr. Tukey also
          developed the Fast Fourier Transform, an algorithm with wide
          application to the physical sciences. It helps astronomers, for
          example, determine the spectrum of light coming from a star more
          quickly than previously possible. 

          As his career progressed, he also became a hub for other
scientists.
          He was part of a group of Princeton professors that gathered
          regularly and included Lyman Spitzer Jr., who inspired the Hubble
          Space Telescope. Mr. Tukey also persuaded a group of the nation's
          top statisticians to spend a year at Princeton in the early 1970's
          working together on robust analysis problems, said David C.
          Hoaglin, a former student of Mr. Tukey. 

          Mr. Tukey was a consultant to the Educational Testing Service, the
          Xerox Corporation and Merck & Company. From 1960 to 1980, he
          helped design the polls that the NBC television network used to
          predict and analyze elections. 

          His first brush with publicity came in 1950, when the National
          Research Council appointed him to a committee to evaluate the
          Kinsey Report, which shocked many Americans by describing the
          country's sexual habits as far more diverse than had been thought.
          From their first meeting, when Mr. Kinsey told Mr. Tukey to stop
          singing a Gilbert and Sullivan tune aloud while working, the two
          men clashed, according to "Alfred C. Kinsey," a biography by James
          H. Jones. 

          In a series of meetings over two years, Mr. Kinsey vigorously
          defended his work, which Mr. Tukey believed was seriously flawed,
          relying on a sample of people who knew each other. Mr. Tukey said
          a random selection of three people would have been better than a
          group of 300 chosen by Mr. Kinsey.

> From: "Dieter Ramseier" <ramseier at geobot.umnw.ethz.ch>
> Date: Fri, 28 Jul 2000 14:29:17 +0200

> 
> I used a split-split-plot design in an experiment. The analysis with S-Plus
> works well, but unfortunatelly I am not able to get multiple comparisons.
> The formula I used is:
> 
> konk.aov <- aov(Mean1 ~ Block + (C+N+G)*Species + (C:N) + (C:G) + (N:G) +
> Error(Block/G/(N:C)))
> multicomp(konk.aov, method='bon')

You need to look in the strata, which are separate aov models, for multiple
comparisons within terms.   That is G and C, N, C:G, N:G are in separate
models.

It might have worked, but the strata models are missing the information
you would need.

You can do Bonferroni by hand, but without the pretty plots.

messages.body_plain:
> From: "Peter Wollan" <wollan at mayo.edu>
> Date: Fri, 28 Jul 2000 07:45:46 -0500
> 
> Doesn't anyone find this strange?  I'd have hoped that alternate ways of
> referring to the same object produce the same result.  The good Dr. Ripley
> clearly has some intuition here that I'm missing.

That's the power of S.  A data.frame is both list-like and matrix-like.
$ is list-like
[, ] is matrix-like.

(but [[]] is list-like and different from $ in this case, so I'm relying
on knowing about this anomaly.)

Note from my earlier detailed explanation that S-PLUS 5.1 is, er, 
`less inconsistent'.

[A Perl slogan is `there is more than one way to do it' and somewhere
in the Win32 docs it says in effect `thank goodness, as that gives a
chance that one of them will get the answer you want'.]

Brian

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

thanks to Bill Dunlap and Chuck Taylor, from Mathsoft, for looking into the
problem (see original post following and Bill's reply).
Thanks also to Andreas Krause for supplying a solution, if not an explanation.

If the graphs are sent to a local drive rather than a network drive the file
names are generated as expected, i.e. as claimed in the help file of the
Graphsheet function.  I will leave to others to explain, if they can, why it is
so.

Thanks to all respondents,

Gérald Jean
Analyste-conseil (statistiques), Actuariat
télephone            : (418) 835-4900 poste (7639)
télecopieur          : (418) 835-6657
courrier électronique: gerald.jean at spgdag.ca

"In God we trust all others must bring data"

******************** Original Post

Hello S-users,

I am generating several plots with the .BMP extension to be imported in MS Word.
Everything works fine as long as I have less than 10 pages, each page holds 2
plots (par('mfrow') = c(2, 1)).  The help file for graphsheet says:

"The first sequence of "#" characters will be replaced with a number in the
generated filenames. For instance, the first file generated using a value of
"splus###.wmf" would be "splus001.wmf"."

I have the following code before the loop that generates the plots.

fname <- paste(Plot.file, 'Plot###.', ExportType, sep = '')
graphsheet(format = ExportType, color.style = 'color', background.color =
           'User9', print.background = prt.back,
           color.scheme = 'standard', file = fname)

where Plot.file is a directory name, ExportType = 'BMP' in this case and
prt.back = Tor F.

But the file names generated are NOT:  directory\Plot001.BMP,
directory\Plot002.BMP, etc. as claimed by the help file;
but rather: directory\Plot100.BMP, directory\Plot200.BMP, ...,
directory\Plot900.BMP, directory\Plot100.BMP(this is not a typo, the first
file generated gets overwritten), directory\Plot110.BMP, ...

As in what I am doing now I have only 18 pages of plots I don't know what name
would come out after Plot190.BMP, presumably
Plot200.BMP and the second file generated woul be erased.

Anybody knows what is going on and how to fix this

Thanks for your help,

Gérald Jean

*************************** Bill Dunlap's response

We have seen this once before and haven't been able to track it down
yet.  We cannot reproduce it in house and the other user who complained
was in Basil (Switzerland).  My personal guess is that it has something
to do with French versions of certain DLL's that come with Windows,
but that is nothing more than a hunch.

messages.subject: [S] map projection
messages.body_plain:
I have been having difficulties overlaying data on maps when using a
map projection.  Any sugestions would be appreciated.

I'm using Splus Version 5.1 Release 1 for Sun SPARC.

Here is the best that I have been able to do: (it has to be easier)

----------------------------------------------------
# set limits of map
west=-95
east=10
south=-20
north=60

# make some data: x is longitude, y is latitude
x <- c(-60,-50,-40,-30,-20)
y <- c(40,25,0,50,-20)

# compute projected coordinates to plot
merc <- mapproject(x,y,projection="mercator")

# turn on postscript
postscript(file = "test.eps", horizontal = F)

# set aspect ratio:  seems to be necessary
#                    and a black art (this value is a guess)
#               scaling is also a guess
par(pin=c(7.0,6.6)/1.1)

# plot without axes
#     note the shift of data by 0.045.   ?????
#          this value was found to be needed to get data alligned properly
plot(merc$x+0.045,merc$y,axes=F,
     xlim=c(mapproject(west,south)$x,mapproject(east,north)$x),
     ylim=c(mapproject(west,south)$y,mapproject(east,north)$y),
     xlab="longitude (degrees)",
     ylab="latitude (degrees)",
     main="test")

# add map
map("world.thin",projection="mercator",
     xlim=c(west,east),
     ylim=c(south,north),
     interior=F,lwd=0.5,add=T)

# add lower axis
#     note ticks seem to be needed beyond xlim and ylim
#          to get the axes to work right
# note also that I can't raise the xlab
axis(1, at=mapproject(c(west-5,
                        west+15+((east-west-25)/4)*(0:4),
                        east+5),0:6)$x,  
        mgp=c(0,0.9,0),
        labels=c("","80W","60W","40W","20W","0","")) 

# add left axis --- same problem
axis(2, at=mapproject(0:6,c(south-5,
                            south+((north-south)/4)*(0:4),
                            north+5))$y, 
        mgp=c(3,1.5,0),
        labels=c("","20S","0","20N","40N","60N","")) 

# add upper axis, no labels --- same problem
axis(3, at=mapproject(c(west-5,
                        west+15+((east-west-25)/4)*(0:4),
                        east+5),0:6)$x, 
        labels=rep("",7))

# add right axis, no labels --- same problem
axis(4, at=mapproject(1:7,c(south-5,
                            south+((north-south)/4)*(0:4),
                            north+5))$y, 
        labels=rep("",7))

# turn off postscript
dev.off()

----------------------------------------------------

In trellis, I don't get that far:

     map("world.thin",interior=F,lwd=0.5,
            xlim=c(west,east),

            pch="*")
}

# make data frame using same data
test <- data.frame(x=x,y=y)

# make xyplot

trellis.device(device = postscript, horizontal = F, file = "test.eps")
xyplot(y~x,
        data = test,
        main = "XBT locations using mercator projection",
       panel = panel.map)
dev.off()

messages.subject: Re: [S] definition of "loess()"
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-Plus users,
E-mail:  s-news at wubios.wustl.edu 

Hi!

   I appreciate comments from Dr. Gregory L. Snow and Dr. Andy I. Liaw 
about my question on "interpolation by loess()". I derived a conclusion on this 
matter
as below. If someone makes additional comments on this, please send
it directly to my E-mail address(takezawa at affrc.go.jp)

   Interpolation by "loess()" is possible, while interpolation by LOESS is 
mathematically impossible. This is due to a useful feature of "lsfit()" .

Example:
   lsfit(x=c(1,2,3), y=c(2,3,4), w=c(0,1,0))

The command above is mathematically nonsense because only one
point is given to obtain a "y=ax+b equation". However,
lsfit() results in "y=3"; it actually passes through the second points.
   This feature of "lsfit()" realizes interpolation by "loess()",
though I guess that not so many people use "loess()" for interpolation.

   

   *****    Kunio Takezawa, Ph.D. (takezawa at affrc.go.jp)    *****

messages.subject: [S] Re: definition of "loess()"
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-Plus users,
E-mail:  s-news at wubios.wustl.edu 

Hi!

   I really appreciate Dr. Gregory Snow(E-mail: gsnow at splus.mathsoft.com) 
sending me the program below. This is very helpful for understanding how 
"loess()"
works.
   As for interpolation using "loess()", my conclusion is that it is possible
but it is not practical unless predictors are equi-spaced.If someone makes 
additional comments on this, please send it directly to my E-mail 
address(takezawa at affrc.go.jp)

---------- Dr. Gregory Snow's program ----------
loess.demo <- function(x,y,span=2/3,xlim,ylim){
        
        if(span>1){ warning("span reduced to 1 for demo"); span <- 1 }
        
        tmp <- loess.smooth(x,y,span, family="gaussian")
        xl <- range(x,tmp$x)
        xl <- xl + c(-1,1)*0.03*diff(xl)
        yl <- range(y,tmp$y)
        yl <- yl + c(-1,1)*0.05*diff(yl)
        
        scatter.smooth(x,y,span, xlab="x", ylab="y",pch=".",xlim=xl,
        ylim=yl,family="gaussian")
        
        repeat {
                x0 <- locator(1)$x
                if (length(x0) < 1) break
                        
                q <- as.integer(span*length(x))
                
                d <- sort( abs( x-x0 ) )[q]
                
                w <- rep(0, length(x))
                s <- abs(x-x0) <= d 
                w[s] <- (1-(abs(x[s]-x0)/d)^3)^3
        

        scatter.smooth(x,y,span, xlab="x",
ylab="y",pch=".",xlim=xl,ylim=yl,family="gaussian")

                symbols(x,y,circle=sqrt(w), inches=.3, add=T, col=6)
                abline(lsfit(x,y,w), col=5)
                abline(v=x0,col=5)
                
                if( x0-d > xl[1] ) abline(v=x0-d, col=5, lty=2)
                if( x0+d < xl[2] ) abline(v=x0+d, col=5, lty=2)
                
        }
}
---------- End of Dr. Gregory Snow's program ----------

   *****    Kunio Takezawa, Ph.D. (takezawa at affrc.go.jp)    *****
  *****            Research Information Section              *****
 **** Hokuriku National Agricultural Experiment Station, JAPAN ****

fundamental -- I'd never had that particular case in the test suite, the
if-then-else structure of the routine doesn't cover this case, and you
are seeing an error message that amounts to "I'm confused".
